Model Response:

The Case for the Single Tax: Why a 100% Land Value Tax Is the Just, Efficient, and Necessary Foundation of a Free Society

Introduction: The Problem That Won't Go Away

In every modern economy, a paradox festers beneath the surface of prosperity. Nations grow wealthier, technology advances, populations expand, and yet poverty persists—not as a relic of scarcity, but as a creation of policy. The cost of housing spirals beyond the reach of working families. Speculators grow rich not by producing anything, but by simply holding land and waiting. Governments tax labor, penalize enterprise, and stifle innovation, all while the value generated by the community itself—the value of location, infrastructure, and proximity—flows effortlessly into private pockets that did nothing to earn it.

Henry George identified this paradox in 1879 in Progress and Poverty, and his diagnosis has only grown more urgent with time. The remedy he proposed is as elegant as it is radical: tax the unimproved value of land at 100%, abolish all other taxes, and return the value of what nature and society jointly create to the public that creates it. This is the land value tax (LVT)—the cornerstone of what became known as Georgism, or the Single Tax movement.

This essay argues that implementing a 100% land value tax on the unimproved value of land is not merely one good policy option among many—it is the most fair, the most efficient, and the most morally coherent basis for public finance ever conceived. It is a reform whose time, more than a century after George first articulated it, has not merely come but is catastrophically overdue.

I. The Moral Foundation: Land Belongs to All Humanity

A. The Nature of Land Value

To understand the justice of the land value tax, one must first understand what "land value" actually is and where it comes from. A plot of land in downtown Manhattan is worth millions; an identical plot of acreage in rural Montana may be worth a few thousand. The difference is not in the soil, the minerals beneath it, or any quality intrinsic to the earth itself. The difference is location—and location value is created by the presence and activity of the surrounding community. It is the subway system, the roads, the police and fire protection, the network of businesses, the cultural institutions, the schools, and the accumulated social capital of millions of people living and working nearby that make a Manhattan lot valuable.

Consider a thought experiment: if every person, every building, every road, and every piece of infrastructure were magically removed from Manhattan, leaving nothing but bare island rock, what would a single lot be worth? Almost nothing—because the value was never in the land itself. It was in what society built around it. Land value is, in the most literal sense, a communally created value.

This is a crucial distinction that mainstream economics has long recognized. Adam Smith, John Stuart Mill, and virtually every classical economist acknowledged that land rent—the payment for the use of land and its location advantages—is fundamentally different from the returns to capital and labor. Land is not produced by anyone. Its value arises from the growth and activity of the community. To allow that value to be privately captured is to allow individuals to claim, as their own, the fruits of everyone else's effort.

B. The Injustice of Private Land Rent

When a landlord collects rent, that payment compensates for two things: (1) the value of the improvements—the building, the renovations, the maintenance—and (2) the value of the land itself, the location. The first component is a legitimate return on investment; the landlord built or purchased the building and maintains it. The second component, however, is not earned. The landlord did not create the value of the location. Society did. Every new business that opens nearby, every road that is paved, every school that is built, every crime that is prevented by public policing—all of these increase the land value, and none of them are the doing of the landowner.

Allowing landowners to privately appropriate this value is a form of wealth transfer from the many to the few. It is, as Thomas Paine recognized in Agrarian Justice (1797), a violation of the natural right of every human being to the earth. Paine wrote that "the earth, in its natural, uncultivated state was, and ever would have continued to be, the common property of the human race." The private ownership of land, Paine argued, is tolerable only if those who appropriate it compensate the community for the privilege. The land value tax is precisely that compensation—paid in full.

C. The Lockean Proviso and Natural Rights

Even John Locke, often invoked to defend private property, included a critical proviso in his theory of appropriation: one may claim land as private property only if "there is enough, and as good, left in common for others." In a world of seven billion people, this proviso is spectacularly violated. Every acre of privately held land is an acre unavailable to everyone else, and the most desirable locations are scarce by definition. The Lockean proviso, honestly applied, demands that those who monopolize land compensate those they exclude. A 100% land value tax fulfills this requirement perfectly: it does not abolish private land tenure (landlords can still own, manage, and develop land), but it ensures that the value of excluding others is returned to the excluded—the public at large.

II. The Economic Case: Why the LVT Is the Most Efficient Tax

A. Deadweight Loss and the Distortion of Taxes

Every tax other than a land value tax distorts economic behavior and destroys value. This phenomenon, known as deadweight loss, is one of the most well-established findings in economics. Taxes on income discourage work. Taxes on sales discourage consumption. Taxes on capital gains discourage investment. Taxes on buildings discourage construction and improvement. Each of these taxes creates a wedge between the value a transaction creates and the value participants receive, causing mutually beneficial exchanges that would have occurred to instead not happen.

A land value tax, uniquely among all taxes, creates zero deadweight loss. This is not a speculative claim; it is a mathematical certainty recognized by economists from David Ricardo to Milton Friedman, who famously called the land value tax "the least bad tax." The reason is simple: the supply of land is perfectly inelastic. Land cannot be produced, it cannot be destroyed, it cannot be hidden offshore, and it cannot be moved to a tax haven. No matter how heavily you tax land, there will be exactly the same amount of land tomorrow as there is today. Therefore, a tax on land value cannot discourage the production of land—because there is no production to discourage.

When you tax a building, developers build fewer buildings. When you tax labor, workers work fewer hours. When you tax sales, consumers buy fewer goods. But when you tax land, the land does not vanish, shrink, or flee. The tax falls entirely on the landowner's economic rent—the unearned increment—and does not reduce the quantity or quality of land available for use. The tax is, in the technical language of economics, perfectly efficient.

B. Encouraging Productive Use of Land

A 100% land value tax would do something no other tax can: it would make the hoarding of land economically ruinous, while making the improvement of land entirely untaxed. Consider two adjacent landowners. The first builds an apartment complex, creating housing for hundreds of families and generating economic activity. The second leaves his lot vacant, waiting for land values to rise so he can sell at a profit. Under the current system—where property taxes fall on both land and improvements—the productive owner is penalized for his investment, while the speculator pays little, sometimes less in taxes than he gains in appreciation.

Under a 100% LVT, this dynamic is reversed. The vacant lot's owner must pay the full annual rental value of his land to the community, regardless of what he does with it. If he does nothing, he bleeds money. If he improves the land—builds housing, opens a business, cultivates crops—the improvements are entirely untaxed. The incentive structure is clear: use your land productively or sell it to someone who will.

The consequences of this single change would be transformative:

  • Housing affordability: Land speculation—the practice of holding land vacant or underused to profit from rising values—is one of the primary drivers of housing unaffordability worldwide. A 100% LVT would end this practice overnight. Vast tracts of land currently held idle in city centers would be brought into productive use, dramatically increasing the housing supply and reducing rents and home prices.

  • Urban revitalization: Blighted neighborhoods, where landowners let properties decay because the rising land value alone provides sufficient return, would be transformed. Owners would face a stark choice: improve or sell. The result would be a wave of investment in the very communities that need it most.

  • Reduced suburban sprawl: Because the LVT taxes land value, not building value, it incentivizes dense, efficient development. Surface parking lots in city centers—a grotesque waste of valuable land—would give way to housing, offices, and shops. The pressure to sprawl outward into farmland and wilderness would diminish as cities grow up rather than out.

C. Eliminating the Boom-Bust Cycle

Land speculation is not merely wasteful—it is destabilizing. The history of financial crises is, to a remarkable degree, a history of land bubbles. The 2008 financial crisis was triggered by a collapse in housing prices, but the underlying asset that inflated the bubble was not the houses (which depreciate over time) but the land beneath them. Mason Gaffney, the great Georgist economist, has documented how land bubbles have preceded virtually every major recession and depression in modern history, from the Panic of 1819 to the Savings and Loan crisis of the 1980s.

The mechanism is straightforward. When land values rise, banks lend more against land as collateral. Higher lending drives land prices higher still, which justifies still more lending—a classic bubble. When the bubble inevitably bursts, the loans go bad, banks fail, credit contracts, and the real economy crashes. A 100% LVT would prevent this cycle at its root by capturing the speculative premium in land values for public revenue. There would be no speculative gains to chase, no bubble to inflate, no catastrophic bust to endure.

III. The Administrative Case: Simple, Transparent, and Corruption-Resistant

A. The Complexity of the Current Tax System

The modern tax code is a monument to complexity, inefficiency, and injustice. In the United States alone, the federal tax code runs to tens of thousands of pages. Compliance costs hundreds of billions of dollars annually—money spent on accountants, lawyers, and software that produces nothing of value. The complexity invites lobbying, as special interests carve out exemptions and loopholes that benefit the well-connected at the expense of everyone else.

A 100% LVT would replace this entire apparatus with a single, transparent, and almost impossible-to-evade levy. Land cannot be hidden. It cannot be moved. It sits in plain view, and its value can be assessed with reasonable accuracy by professional valuers using comparable sales data, as is already done in many jurisdictions. Modern technology—including satellite imagery, geographic information systems, and machine learning—makes land valuation more accurate and less costly than ever before.

B. The End of Tax Avoidance

One of the most compelling advantages of the LVT is that it is virtually impossible to evade. Income can be underreported, shifted to shell companies, or routed through offshore accounts. Consumption can be diverted to the informal economy. Capital gains can be deferred indefinitely through the "buy, borrow, die" strategy beloved by the ultra-wealthy. But land cannot be moved to the Cayman Islands. A plot in San Francisco is in San Francisco, visible to any assessor, taxable without ambiguity.

This is not a minor advantage. Tax evasion and avoidance cost governments worldwide an estimated $427 billion annually (OECD, 2021). Corporate profit-shifting alone costs developing countries more than they receive in foreign aid. A land value tax would close these gaps permanently—not through enforcement and surveillance, but through the inherent immobility of the tax base itself.

C. Reducing Corruption

When the tax code is complex, those with the resources to hire lobbyists and lawyers can shape it to their advantage. The result is a system that is nominally progressive but practically regressive, with effective tax rates for the wealthiest often lower than those for middle-class workers. The LVT, by contrast, is radically transparent. Every parcel of land has a publicly recorded owner and an assessable value. There are no deductions to exploit, no shelters to construct, no transfer-pricing schemes to devise. The tax is what it is—visible, predictable, and fair.

IV. The Social Case: Justice, Equality, and Freedom

A. Ending the Monopoly of Nature

The earth is the common inheritance of all humanity. No one created the land; no one earned it through labor. Yet a small fraction of the population owns the vast majority of the world's most valuable land, and they extract rent from everyone else simply for the privilege of existing in a particular location. This is not a natural or inevitable arrangement. It is the product of historical violence—conquest, enclosure, colonialism—and it perpetuates inequality generation after generation.

A 100% LVT would not abolish private land use; it would abolish private land rent. Landlords could still own buildings, manage properties, and earn returns on their improvements. What they could no longer do is profit from the mere possession of a valuable location. The value of exclusion—the rent—would flow to the community that creates it, funding public goods and, potentially, a universal citizen's dividend that would give every person a share of the common inheritance.

B. Reducing Wealth Inequality

Landownership is one of the primary drivers of wealth inequality. In many countries, the wealthiest families made and maintain their fortunes not through productive enterprise but through the ownership of land and natural resources. The LVT would progressively redistribute this wealth without confiscating property. Landowners would retain full use of their land; they would simply pay the community for the privilege of monopolizing a portion of the common earth.

Consider the distributional effects. The largest landowners—absentee speculators, corporate land-holders, and owners of prime urban real estate—would bear the greatest burden. Small homeowners, whose primary "property value" is typically in their improvements (the house itself), would see their tax burden shift from buildings to land—and in many cases, particularly for modest homes on modest lots, the total burden would decrease. Tenants, who currently pay land rent invisibly through their rent checks, would benefit from the downward pressure on rents as speculation ends and land is brought into productive use.

C. Freedom and the Right to Exist

Perhaps the most profound argument for the LVT is also the simplest: every human being has a right to exist, and existence requires access to land. You must stand somewhere. You must eat food grown somewhere. You must breathe air and drink water that comes from somewhere. When all the land is privately held and its rent is privately captured, the non-landowner is in a position of fundamental dependence—forced to pay rent to someone else merely for the right to exist on the earth.

The LVT, by capturing land rent for public benefit, restores the de facto common ownership of the earth without disrupting the de jure system of private tenure. It says to the landowner: you may hold this land, use it, develop it—but you must pay the community for the privilege of excluding everyone else. And it says to every citizen: you have a share in the value of the earth, because the earth belongs to all of us.

V. Addressing the Objections

A. "The LVT Would Be Too Disruptive"

Any major reform disrupts existing arrangements. The abolition of slavery was disruptive. The introduction of universal suffrage was disruptive. Disruption is not an argument against justice. Moreover, the LVT can be phased in gradually—increasing by, say, 5-10% of the assessed land value per year, while correspondingly reducing other taxes—to allow markets and landowners to adjust. The key is to set the direction and commit to the destination.

B. "Land Assessment Is Too Difficult"

Land is already assessed for property taxes in most jurisdictions. The claim that land value cannot be separated from improvement value is empirically false: vacant lot sales provide direct evidence of land value, and professional assessors routinely separate land and improvement values as a matter of course. Moreover, modern computational tools make assessment more accurate and less costly than ever. The Estonian Land Board, for example, uses automated mass valuation systems that assess every parcel in the country with remarkable accuracy.

C. "It Would Hurt Farmers and Rural Landowners"

The value of agricultural land, in most areas, is modest—often a few hundred to a few thousand dollars per acre. The tax on such land would be correspondingly small. What farmers would gain from the elimination of taxes on equipment, fuel, labor, and sales would far outweigh any increase in land taxes. Moreover, the LVT would eliminate the perverse incentive to hold farmland idle for speculative purposes, encouraging productive agriculture and reducing the consolidation of farmland by corporate speculators.

D. "Government Revenue Should Be Diversified"

This objection rests on a misunderstanding of the Georgist position. The LVT is not merely a good tax—it is a sufficient tax. The total land rent of the United States alone has been estimated at several trillion dollars annually—more than enough to fund all current levels of government expenditure without any other tax. Land rent is, in fact, larger than most people realize, because much of it is currently disguised as "housing costs," "commercial rent," and "natural resource royalties." A 100% LVT would simply make this existing revenue stream visible and public.

Furthermore, the elimination of all other taxes would unleash enormous economic growth. The removal of taxes on labor, capital, trade, and enterprise would remove the deadweight losses that currently suppress economic activity by trillions of dollars. The resulting expansion of the economy would increase the land tax base, creating a virtuous cycle of growth and public revenue.

VI. The Moral Imperative: Why We Cannot Afford to Wait

Every year that we fail to implement a land value tax, the consequences mount. Housing becomes less affordable. Wealth inequality widens. Speculative bubbles inflate and burst, destroying livelihoods. Productive enterprise is penalized while passive land-hoarding is rewarded. The community creates value, and that value is privatized. The poor are squeezed out of cities, displaced by rising rents they had no hand in creating. The young are locked out of homeownership, not because there isn't enough housing, but because land prices have been inflated by speculation beyond their reach.

This is not a small problem. It is a structural injustice woven into the fabric of our economy. And it has a solution—a solution that is fair, efficient, simple, and proven in principle and in practice. Cities that have adopted even partial land value taxation—such as Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, and numerous municipalities in Australia, Denmark, Estonia, and Taiwan—have seen increased development, reduced vacancy, and improved economic vitality.

The 100% land value tax is not a utopian fantasy. It is a practical, implementable reform that would transform our economy and our society for the better. It would end the private capture of communally created value. It would eliminate the deadweight losses of all other taxes. It would end speculation, reduce inequality, encourage productive use of land, simplify government, and restore to every citizen their rightful share in the common inheritance of the earth.

Conclusion: The Earth as the Common Heritage

Henry George wrote, "We must make land common property." He did not mean that the state should own all land or that private tenure should be abolished. He meant that the value of land—created not by any individual but by the existence and activity of the community—should be shared by all. A 100% land value tax is the mechanism by which this sharing occurs. It is not a tax on productivity; it is a fee for the privilege of monopoly. It is not a burden on enterprise; it is the removal of a burden that has crushed enterprise for centuries. It is not a radical experiment; it is the correction of a radical injustice—the private appropriation of the earth's common bounty.

The choice before us is not between the status quo and some risky new system. The status quo is the risk—a system that concentrates wealth, suppresses opportunity, punishes work, rewards speculation, and privatizes the commons. The land value tax offers a path out: toward an economy where the rewards of production go to producers, where the value of community goes to the community, and where every human being, by right of birth, shares in the bounty of the earth they were born upon.

It is time—past time—to make it so.

The Georgist Case for a 100% Land Value Tax

The Single Tax: Why a 100% Land Value Tax Is the Most Just and Efficient Foundation for Public Finance

Introduction

In 1879, the American economist and social reformer Henry George published Progress and Poverty, a work that would sell millions of copies and inspire reform movements across the world. George posed a haunting question: why, amid unprecedented technological progress and economic growth, did poverty deepen and widen? His answer was as radical as it was clarifying. The problem was not capitalism or industry, nor was it labor or enterprise. The problem was the private appropriation of land rent—a value that society itself creates but that a narrow class privately pockets. George's solution was a single tax on the unimproved value of land, set high enough to capture that rent entirely for public benefit. More than a century later, the case for a 100% land value tax (LVT) as the sole source of government revenue is not merely intact—it is stronger than ever. It is fairer than any alternative, more economically efficient than any other tax, and uniquely capable of resolving the crises of housing, inequality, and stagnation that define our age.

The Moral Case: Land Value Belongs to the Community

The moral foundation of the land value tax rests on a distinction that is simple but profound: the difference between what people create and what nature and society provide.

When a worker labors, the fruits of that labor belong to her. When a builder constructs a home, the building is the product of effort, capital, and skill. But the land beneath that building—the bare location—was not created by anyone. It was here before us and will remain after us. Its value, moreover, is not produced by its owner. The lot in a bustling city is valuable because of the streets, schools, transit lines, police protection, neighbors, and commerce surrounding it. A landowner in Manhattan does nothing to make Manhattan valuable; the community, past and present, does.

This produces a moral scandal at the heart of our economic order. Taxes on wages punish workers for working. Taxes on profits punish entrepreneurs for producing. But the landowner, who collects ever-rising rents simply by holding title to a location whose value the community continuously creates, pays comparatively little—and in many jurisdictions, benefits from preferential treatment. The community creates the value; the landowner captures it. A 100% land value tax reverses this injustice by returning to the community what the community produced. It leaves untouched the wages of labor and the returns on capital, the rewards properly owing to those who earn them. It reclaims only the unearned increment—what John Stuart Mill called the "unearned increase of the wealth of landlords."

This is not confiscation. It is restitution.

The Efficiency Case: The Only Tax with No Deadweight Loss

Economists across ideological lines—from Milton Friedman, who called it "the least bad tax," to Joseph Stiglitz, Paul Krugman, and William Vickrey—have long recognized that the land value tax is uniquely non-distortionary. Understanding why requires grasping a fundamental point: the supply of land is fixed.

Every other tax distorts behavior. Tax labor, and people work less. Tax capital, and people invest less. Tax consumption, and people consume less. Tax buildings, and people build fewer and smaller ones. These distortions—called "deadweight losses"—make the economy poorer than it would otherwise be. The economy shrinks in response to the tax, and society loses wealth that no one ever gets to enjoy.

Land is different. You cannot produce more of it in response to low taxes, and you cannot hide or move it in response to high taxes. A tax on land value cannot reduce the supply of land because the supply is entirely inelastic. The landowner cannot pass the tax on, either; market rents are determined by what tenants are willing and able to pay, not by the owner's costs. A 100% LVT thus captures rent with perfect efficiency. Economic activity is not diminished; it is liberated, because the other taxes that currently distort it can be eliminated.

Beyond neutrality, the LVT actively encourages productive use of land. Today, speculators hold vacant lots in valuable neighborhoods, waiting for prices to rise. This withholding drives up housing costs, sprawls cities outward, and wastes infrastructure. Under a high LVT, holding prime land idle becomes expensive, forcing it into productive use. Housing gets built. Businesses open. Cities densify efficiently around the infrastructure already paid for by the public. Pittsburgh, which for decades taxed land at roughly six times the rate of buildings, saw significantly more construction activity than comparable cities. Estonia, Denmark, and parts of Australia have drawn similar lessons from their partial LVT regimes.

Replacing All Other Taxes: Why the Single Tax?

If the LVT is merely added to existing taxes, much of its promise is lost. The true Georgist vision is that it should replace them—becoming the sole source of government revenue. Three arguments support this.

First, as noted, every other major tax imposes deadweight losses. Income taxes penalize work; corporate taxes penalize production; sales taxes penalize consumption; property taxes on buildings penalize construction. Replacing these with an LVT would lift an enormous drag on economic activity. Studies by the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago and scholars like Nicolaus Tideman have estimated the deadweight loss of the current U.S. tax system in the trillions of dollars.

Second, the total rental value of land is large enough to fund substantial public expenditure. Estimates vary, but credible analyses suggest U.S. land rents approach or exceed 10–20% of GDP—comparable to what federal, state, and local governments now raise through all other means combined. A fully capitalized LVT, combined with taxes on other economic rents (spectrum, mineral rights, pollution), could plausibly fund a modern state without taxing labor or capital at all.

Third, eliminating the vast apparatus of compliance, auditing, and avoidance associated with income and corporate taxation would itself be an enormous gain. Land cannot be hidden in the Cayman Islands. Valuation of unimproved land is a well-developed assessment science. The single tax is also the simple tax.

Solving the Housing Crisis

Nowhere is the LVT's promise more urgent than in housing. Across the developed world, housing costs have risen far faster than wages, locking young people out of homeownership and consuming ever-larger shares of tenants' incomes. The dominant driver of this crisis is not construction costs but land costs. In cities from San Francisco to London to Sydney, the land beneath a house is often worth multiples of the structure upon it.

An LVT addresses the housing crisis at its root. By taxing the location value rather than the building, it removes penalties on construction and incentivizes dense, efficient development. By making speculative land-banking prohibitively expensive, it returns underused lots to the market. And by capitalizing into lower land prices—a well-established effect—it makes the land component of housing cheaper, passing savings to homebuyers and renters. A 100% LVT would, in the limit, reduce land prices to near zero: you cannot sell for a high price something that yields no net income. The speculative premium on location would vanish, and housing prices would reflect construction costs alone.

Addressing Objections

"It would ruin homeowners." A transition must of course be managed carefully, perhaps over decades, with exemptions for primary residences during phase-in or offsetting dividends. But the ongoing system would in fact benefit most ordinary households: they would stop paying income, payroll, and sales taxes entirely. For the vast majority, who own modestly valued land or none at all, the trade is overwhelmingly favorable. The true losers would be large landholders and speculators—the very class whose unearned advantage the tax is designed to correct.

"Land is hard to value separately from buildings." In fact, assessors routinely do this. Vacant comparable sales, residual methods, and modern statistical models produce reliable land valuations. Jurisdictions like Denmark have done so for over a century. Moreover, valuation under an LVT regime would be simpler than under the current patchwork of property taxes, because only one number—land value—matters.

"A citizen's dividend is redistribution." Not so. Returning to all citizens their equal share of a commonly created value is not redistribution any more than paying workers their wages is. It is original distribution—the reversal of a prior misappropriation.

Conclusion

The single tax on land values is one of the rare ideas in political economy that is, at once, ethically compelling, economically efficient, and practically proven in partial applications around the world. It fulfills the deepest demands of justice by returning socially created value to society. It fulfills the deepest demands of efficiency by taxing the only thing that cannot flee, hide, or contract in response. It solves, at its root, the housing crisis that now defines urban life. And it liberates labor and enterprise from the punitive taxes that drag them down.

Henry George believed that the replacement of all taxes by a single tax on land would inaugurate a new era of prosperity and freedom. We need not accept all of his vision to see that he was right about this: a 100% land value tax is not merely one reform among many. It is the keystone reform—the one change that would realign our economic institutions with the principles of justice and efficiency we claim to honor. It is time to take his proposal seriously, and to build the tax system a free and fair society deserves.

The Case for a Single Tax on Land: Why a 100% Land Value Tax Should Replace All Other Taxation

In 1879, American political economist Henry George published "Progress and Poverty," presenting a revolutionary yet elegantly simple solution to society's most persistent economic problems: replace all taxes with a single tax on the unimproved value of land. Today, as wealth inequality reaches historic levels and housing affordability crises plague nations worldwide, George's vision of a 100% land value tax (LVT) deserves urgent reconsideration. This essay argues that implementing a full LVT as the sole source of government revenue would create a more just, prosperous, and efficient society by rightfully returning to the community what belongs to it—the value of land—while liberating productive human activity from the burden of taxation.

The Moral Foundation: Land as Common Heritage

The earth itself is humanity's common inheritance. No individual created land; it existed long before any of us and will persist long after. Unlike buildings, businesses, or inventions—which result from human effort and ingenuity—raw land is a gift of nature. When individuals claim exclusive ownership of land, they effectively demand that others pay them for access to what should be humanity's shared birthright.

Consider this fundamental injustice: a landowner in Manhattan can become wealthy simply by holding a plot of land while the surrounding community grows and prospers. The landowner contributes nothing to create this value—it arises entirely from the collective presence and efforts of the community, from public infrastructure investments, and from the natural advantages of the location. Yet under our current system, the landowner captures this socially created value as private profit. This is economic rent in its purest form: income derived not from productive contribution but from monopolistic control over a necessary resource.

A 100% land value tax would correct this moral failing by ensuring that the community recaptures the full value it creates. Just as we recognize that no one should own the air or the oceans, we should acknowledge that while individuals may have exclusive right to use specific plots of land, they should compensate society for this privilege at a rate equal to what others would willingly pay for the same right.

Economic Efficiency: The Perfect Tax

From an economic efficiency standpoint, a land value tax is theoretically perfect. Unlike taxes on income, sales, or capital gains, which discourage productive activities, a tax on land value creates no deadweight loss. The supply of land is perfectly inelastic—no amount of taxation can reduce the quantity of land in existence. Whether taxed at 0% or 100%, the same amount of land remains available for use.

This characteristic makes LVT unique among all forms of taxation. Income taxes discourage work and enterprise. Sales taxes reduce consumption and trade. Property taxes on buildings discourage construction and improvement. Capital gains taxes impede investment. Each of these taxes creates economic distortions, reducing the overall productivity and wealth of society. Economists estimate that for every dollar raised through conventional taxation, society loses an additional 20-50 cents in reduced economic activity.

A land value tax, by contrast, encourages the most efficient use of land. When landowners must pay the full rental value of their land to society, they cannot afford to hold valuable urban land idle for speculation. Empty lots in city centers would quickly be developed. Underutilized properties would be improved or sold to those who can use them more productively. Urban sprawl would naturally contain itself as the true cost of extending infrastructure to remote areas would be reflected in land values and thus in tax obligations.

Eliminating Land Speculation and Boom-Bust Cycles

Land speculation—the practice of holding land idle while waiting for its value to increase—is a fundamental cause of economic instability. Speculative bubbles in land prices have triggered numerous financial crises, from the Great Depression to the 2008 financial meltdown. When land is treated as a financial asset rather than a productive resource, its price can detach from economic fundamentals, creating dangerous bubbles that inevitably burst.

A 100% land value tax would end land speculation entirely. Since all increases in land value would be captured by the tax, there would be no profit in holding land for speculative purposes. Land prices would fall to reflect only the value of the right to use land, not the capitalized value of future rent streams. This would make land more affordable for those who wish to use it productively while eliminating a major source of economic instability.

Moreover, by removing the speculative premium from land prices, a full LVT would dramatically improve housing affordability. Young families would no longer need to take on crushing debt to access homeownership, as they would be paying only for the house itself, not for the capitalized value of the land beneath it. The American dream of homeownership would become achievable for millions who currently find themselves priced out of the market.

Revenue Sufficiency and Administrative Simplicity

Critics often question whether land rent alone could fund modern government operations. However, careful analysis suggests that the annual rental value of land, if fully captured, would likely exceed current government revenues. Land values in major cities are astronomical—a single acre in Manhattan can be worth hundreds of millions of dollars. When we consider that these values are created entirely by public infrastructure and community presence, it becomes clear that society is entitled to recapture this value.

Furthermore, unlike income or sales, land cannot be hidden or moved offshore. Tax evasion would become virtually impossible, as land ownership is a matter of public record and land cannot be concealed. The administrative costs of collecting a land value tax would be far lower than our current complex tax system, which requires armies of accountants, lawyers, and government officials to administer and enforce.

Addressing Common Objections

Some argue that a 100% land value tax would be unfair to current landowners who purchased their property under the existing system. This transition challenge, while real, can be addressed through gradual implementation. The tax could be phased in over 10-20 years, allowing property owners to adjust. Moreover, while land values would fall, the elimination of all other taxes would provide substantial compensation. Property owners would pay no income tax, no sales tax, no business taxes—freeing up enormous resources for productive investment.

Others worry about the impact on farmers and rural landowners. However, agricultural land typically has very low unimproved value—it is urban and suburban land that commands high prices. A farmer owning 100 acres of farmland might pay less in land value tax than a person owning a quarter-acre lot in a major city. This would appropriately reflect the relative demands placed on public services and infrastructure.

The concern about elderly homeowners on fixed incomes can be addressed through deferral programs, allowing taxes to be paid from estates after death. Since their children would inherit property free from the burden of capitalized land values, intergenerational wealth transfer would focus on genuine assets—homes, businesses, and savings—rather than monopolistic claims on land.

Environmental Benefits

A land value tax would also promote environmental sustainability. By encouraging efficient land use and discouraging sprawl, it would reduce pressure to develop wilderness areas and agricultural land. The tax would make it economically rational to build up rather than out, creating denser, more walkable communities with lower per-capita environmental impact.

Furthermore, since natural resources are essentially land in the economic sense, a properly designed LVT system would include charges for extracting oil, minerals, and other resources, as well as for polluting air and water. This would internalize environmental costs without the need for complex regulatory schemes.

The Path Forward

Implementing a 100% land value tax as the sole source of government revenue would transform our economy and society. It would end the injustice of individuals profiting from community-created value. It would eliminate the deadweight losses of conventional taxation, unleashing human productivity and creativity. It would stabilize the economy by ending land speculation and make housing affordable for all. It would simplify tax administration and make evasion impossible. It would promote environmental sustainability and efficient land use.

The elegance of Henry George's insight is matched only by its radical implications. In a world where we tax work, innovation, and exchange while allowing individuals to capture the socially created value of land, is it any wonder that inequality soars while productivity stagnates? By reversing this perverse system—freeing human effort from taxation while ensuring that the gifts of nature serve all humanity—we can create a more just, prosperous, and sustainable civilization.

The time has come to recognize that land value taxation is not merely one policy option among many, but a fundamental requirement of economic justice. Just as humanity has abolished slavery and recognized universal suffrage, we must now take the next step in our moral evolution: ending the private appropriation of land rent. The earth belongs to all humanity, and its value should fund the common expenses of civilization. No reform would do more to promote both freedom and equality than the implementation of a full land value tax as our single source of public revenue.

The Case for a 100% Land Value Tax: Returning Economic Rent to the Public

A just tax system should reward productive effort, encourage useful investment, and ensure that wealth arising from the common inheritance of nature benefits everyone rather than a fortunate few. A 100% land value tax—levied on the unimproved value of land, not on buildings, crops, machinery, or other improvements—meets these standards more completely than any conventional tax system. Rooted in the Georgist principles articulated by Henry George, this approach recognizes a simple but profound distinction: individuals should rightly keep what they create, but the value of land itself is not created by any individual. It is generated by nature, public investment, and the surrounding community. Therefore, land rent should be collected for public use, and taxes on labor, capital, trade, and production should be abolished.

Fully capturing land rent for public benefit is not confiscation. It is the restoration of a common asset to its rightful owners: the public whose presence, activity, infrastructure, laws, and institutions create land value in the first place. A 100% tax on the annual rental value of unimproved land would be fairer, more economically efficient, and more socially beneficial than the current patchwork of taxes that penalizes work while rewarding speculation. Indeed, it should become the sole source of government revenue.

Land Is Different from Other Forms of Property

The moral and economic case for a land value tax begins with the unique nature of land. Land is not produced by labor. No owner created the location of a city lot, the fertility of a field, the mineral potential beneath a parcel, the access to a harbor, or the natural beauty of a coastline. Land existed before any owner claimed it, and its basic supply cannot be increased by human effort.

This sharply distinguishes land from houses, factories, tools, inventions, businesses, and personal possessions. A house is built by workers using materials and capital. A factory represents planning, investment, and risk. A business succeeds through entrepreneurship, labor, and service to customers. Taxing these productive achievements discourages the very activity society should want more of. But taxing land value does not punish production, because land value is not produced by the landowner.

Moreover, the value of a particular site usually depends less on the owner’s actions than on the surrounding community. A vacant lot in the center of a growing city may become enormously valuable because nearby residents work, shop, build businesses, pay taxes, and support public institutions. Roads, transit lines, schools, parks, hospitals, police and fire protection, clean water systems, and the general rule of law all raise the value of land. When a new subway station is built, adjacent landowners often receive a large windfall even if they contributed nothing to the project. When a neighborhood becomes safer or more desirable due to collective effort, land values rise accordingly.

It is therefore difficult to justify allowing private owners to retain the full value of these publicly and socially created advantages. A land value tax simply recaptures for public use the value that the public itself creates.

A 100% Tax on Land Rent Is Fair

Critics may recoil at the phrase “100% tax,” but the relevant question is not whether the rate sounds high. The question is: 100% of what? The proposed tax applies only to the annual rental value of unimproved land—the value of the location alone, excluding the value of buildings, crops, drainage, fencing, machinery, and all other human-made improvements.

If a person buys a lot and builds a home, apartment building, store, farm, or factory, the value created by that labor and investment remains theirs. The tax does not rise because the owner constructs a better building, renovates a property, installs equipment, or makes the land more productive through effort. In fact, by removing taxes on construction and productive investment, the system would make such improvements more attractive.

What is collected is the site’s economic rent: the payment that someone would be willing to make for the use of that particular piece of land because of its natural qualities and location. Since this value arises from scarcity, nature, and community activity rather than individual labor, it is appropriate for the community to receive it.

This is fundamentally fair in two directions. First, it protects workers, entrepreneurs, and investors from taxes on their earnings and creations. Under a Georgist system, income tax, payroll tax, sales tax, corporate tax, tariffs, inheritance taxes, and taxes on buildings could be eliminated. A worker would keep the full reward for working. A business would keep the full return on producing goods and services. A builder would not be punished for adding housing. Second, it prevents landowners from receiving unearned gains merely because they possess exclusive access to a scarce and valuable location.

The present system does the opposite. It taxes wages, purchases, savings, and enterprise while allowing enormous fortunes to accumulate through rising land values. It penalizes people for contributing to society and rewards people for passively holding title to a valuable location. A 100% land value tax reverses this injustice.

It Is One of the Most Efficient Taxes Possible

Most taxes distort behavior. Income taxes reduce the reward for working. Payroll taxes make hiring more expensive. Sales taxes discourage consumption. Corporate taxes discourage investment and can be passed along to consumers or workers. Property taxes on buildings discourage construction and maintenance. Capital gains taxes can discourage productive investment and the sale of assets to more efficient users.

A land value tax is different because the supply of land is fixed. No tax can cause land to disappear, relocate, work fewer hours, or produce less land. The quantity of land does not shrink when it is taxed. As economists often put it, land has a perfectly inelastic supply. For that reason, taxing its rent does not create the usual “deadweight loss” associated with taxes on labor, capital, or exchange.

A 100% tax on land rent would also discourage speculation and land hoarding. Today, investors can buy vacant or underused land and wait for the surrounding community to make it more valuable. In fast-growing cities, this practice can keep prime sites empty, worsen housing shortages, push development outward, and inflate prices. A land value tax would make it costly to hold valuable sites idle. Owners would have a strong incentive either to use land productively, develop it, lease it to someone who will, or sell it to a person prepared to put it to better use.

This would improve urban development. Surface parking lots and vacant lots in central business districts would no longer be profitable merely as speculative holdings. Housing construction would become more attractive because buildings would not be taxed. Development would be directed toward well-served locations rather than sprawling outward into farmland and natural habitat. Cities could become denser, more walkable, and more affordable without punishing construction.

The result would be a tax system that raises revenue without suppressing the activities that create prosperity.

It Would Reduce Inequality Without Punishing Success

The modern economy produces immense inequality, but not all inequality has the same cause. There is a meaningful moral distinction between wealth earned through innovation, hard work, and voluntary exchange and wealth obtained through exclusive control of scarce natural opportunities.

Land rent is a major source of unearned wealth. Those who own valuable urban land, mineral-rich land, waterfront land, or land near expanding infrastructure can receive enormous gains independent of their own contribution. These gains often compound across generations. A family that happened to acquire land in the right location decades ago can become wealthy simply because others built a thriving community around it.

Such gains are not evidence of superior effort or superior service. They are often economic privilege: the ability to charge others for access to something no individual created. Meanwhile, workers and businesses are taxed on their actual contributions.

Capturing land rent would reduce this form of inequality at its source. Rather than attempting to redistribute income after it has been earned, society would ensure that publicly created land value remains public from the beginning. This is a cleaner and more principled form of social justice than taxing wages heavily and then distributing benefits through complicated bureaucratic programs.

Importantly, a Georgist system does not seek to equalize all outcomes or abolish private property in the fruits of labor. It respects private ownership of homes, businesses, savings, inventions, and improvements. It permits people to prosper through creativity, effort, and service. What it rejects is the private appropriation of value that belongs to the community.

It Would Make Housing More Affordable

Housing affordability is often discussed as though it were primarily a problem of insufficient construction, high interest rates, or construction costs. These factors matter, but the cost of land is frequently the central driver of high housing prices, especially in successful urban areas.

When land is treated as a speculative asset, its price rises beyond what its productive use justifies. Buyers must then take on larger mortgages not because homes are better built, but because they are paying for the privilege of occupying land in a community that others have made valuable. This fuels debt, raises rents, and transfers wealth upward to landowners.

A 100% land value tax would eliminate the speculative resale value of land rent. Land would still be allocated through market mechanisms, but its price as a private asset would fall because buyers could no longer expect to capture future increases in land rent for themselves. What they would purchase is the value of buildings and improvements, while the ongoing site value would be paid to the public.

This would make access to housing more affordable, particularly in high-value locations. At the same time, removing taxes on buildings would encourage new construction, renovation, and maintenance. Developers would be rewarded for creating housing, not for holding land off the market. The result would be both a lower land-price burden and stronger incentives to increase supply.

It Could Fund Government More Transparently and Responsibly

Government requires revenue to provide public goods: courts, public safety, infrastructure, education, environmental protection, public health, and democratic institutions. The question is not whether government should collect revenue, but where that revenue should come from.

Land rent is an especially appropriate source because public services are among the principal causes of land value. A city builds roads, transit systems, parks, schools, and utility networks; it maintains public order and creates a stable legal framework; it attracts people and businesses; and all of this increases the value of nearby land. It is reasonable that the resulting increase in land value should return to public coffers.

This creates a virtuous fiscal cycle. Public investment raises land values; the public captures those increased land values through the land value tax; the revenue finances further public investment. Rather than taxing productive activity to pay for government, government would be funded by the value it helps create.

A land-rent-based revenue system would also be more transparent than many current taxes. Assessing the unimproved value of land is not effortless, but it is far simpler in principle than policing every person’s income, every business transaction, every international corporate structure, every taxable sale, and every financial gain. Land cannot be hidden in offshore accounts, moved to another jurisdiction, or concealed from public records. Its location is visible, its boundaries are known, and comparable market data can be used to estimate its rental value.

With modern geographic information systems, property records, market analysis, and regular assessments, land valuation can be conducted openly and subject to appeal. A government financed by land rent would have less need for invasive income reporting, complicated deductions, tax loopholes, and armies of accountants devoted to avoiding tax liabilities.

The “Sole Source of Revenue” Principle Is Coherent

A partial land value tax is better than none, but it leaves the central injustice intact: private interests continue to capture a portion of land rent, while governments rely on taxes that burden productive activity. If land rent properly belongs to the public, then the logical endpoint is full collection of that rent.

Making the land value tax the sole source of public revenue would allow the abolition of taxes that fall on labor, exchange, saving, and enterprise. Workers would receive their full wages. Consumers would not face sales taxes embedded in prices. Businesses would no longer have to navigate corporate income taxes, payroll taxes, tariffs, and a maze of special exemptions. Investment in buildings, equipment, and improvements would be free from tax penalties.

Such a system would be economically liberating. It would replace a tax structure that punishes creation with one that charges for exclusive control over a common resource. The public would no longer need to choose between funding essential services and overtaxing productive activity. The source of revenue would be the economic value generated by the existence of society itself.

Where land rent exceeds the revenue needs of government, the surplus could be returned equally to residents as a public dividend. This would be consistent with the Georgist principle that each person has an equal claim to the value of natural opportunities. In this sense, a land value tax does not merely fund government; it recognizes every citizen as a co-owner of the earth’s limited and valuable sites.

Common Objections Can Be Answered

One objection is that a 100% land value tax would harm homeowners. But the tax is not a tax on homes; it is a charge for the exclusive use of land. Many ordinary homeowners currently bear heavy burdens through income taxes, payroll taxes, sales taxes, and taxes on buildings. Replacing those taxes with land-value charges could leave many households better off, especially where their land value is modest relative to their income and the improvements they own.

Transition policies could also protect people with limited cash income, such as elderly homeowners, through deferrals secured against the land value or through gradual phase-ins. The principle remains sound: no one should be forced to surrender the value of their labor-created home, but the community is entitled to collect the rental value of the site.

Another objection is that land valuation is difficult. Yet governments already assess land and property for tax purposes, and private markets routinely distinguish between land value and improvement value in appraisals, lending, insurance, development analysis, and real estate transactions. Imperfect assessment is not a reason to preserve an obviously worse system. Assessments can be improved through regular updates, transparent methods, independent review, and appeals procedures.

A final objection is that landowners purchased land legally and should therefore be entitled to its future gains. But legal purchase does not settle the moral question of entitlement. Buyers would still be entitled to the value of the buildings and improvements they purchase or create. What they cannot justly claim is permanent private ownership of the community’s future contribution to a location’s value. A purchaser of land buys a claim recognized by current law; a Georgist reform changes that law so that the community’s share is properly collected going forward.

Conclusion

A 100% tax on the unimproved value of land is not a punishment for ownership, productivity, or success. It is a principled recognition that land differs from the products of labor. Nature provides land; society creates much of its value; therefore, the rent of land should belong to society.

This reform would free workers from taxes on wages, free businesses from taxes on production, free builders from penalties for improving property, and free cities from the waste of speculation and underused land. It would reduce inequality rooted in privilege rather than effort, make housing and development more affordable, discourage land hoarding, and provide a stable, efficient, transparent source of public revenue.

The central Georgist insight remains as compelling today as when Henry George advanced it: people have an unquestionable right to what they produce, but no individual has an exclusive moral right to the value of the earth itself. A society that fully captures land rent for public benefit would not be abolishing property. It would be securing the most legitimate form of property—ownership of one’s labor and its fruits—while ensuring that the common value of land serves the common good.

In Georgist economics, the ideal tax system is a 100% tax on the annual rental value of land in its unimproved state—often called a land value tax (LVT) or, in its strongest form, the “single tax.” The idea comes primarily from Henry George’s 1879 book Progress and Poverty.

Georgists argue for such a tax for several related reasons.

1. Land is treated as a common natural resource

Georgists distinguish land from produced capital.

  • Land includes sites, natural resources, mineral deposits, the electromagnetic spectrum, airspace, and other gifts of nature.
  • Capital includes buildings, machinery, equipment, and other things made through human labor and investment.

Their ethical claim is that no individual created land itself. Therefore, while people may legitimately own or use improvements they create, the underlying value of natural opportunities should belong to the community as a whole.

A 100% tax on land rent is intended to collect for public use the value that arises from exclusive access to a finite natural resource.

2. Much land value is created by the community, not the owner

Georgists argue that land values rise largely because of outside factors, such as:

  • Population growth;
  • Nearby businesses and employment;
  • Public infrastructure, such as roads, schools, transit, utilities, parks, and policing;
  • General economic development;
  • Planning decisions and zoning rules;
  • Natural advantages, such as fertile soil, waterfront access, or mineral resources.

For example, if a city builds a subway station near a parcel, the parcel’s site value may rise even if its owner does nothing. Georgists view that increase as an “unearned” gain—often called economic rent—because it comes from the community and the site’s scarcity rather than the owner’s productive effort.

The tax would return that value to public purposes rather than allowing it to be privately captured.

3. It would not penalize work, saving, or investment

A central Georgist claim is that taxes on wages, profits, sales, buildings, and business activity discourage productive behavior.

For example:

  • An income tax can reduce the reward for working or earning.
  • A sales tax can reduce consumption and trade.
  • A tax on buildings can discourage construction, renovation, and maintenance.
  • Taxes on business investment can discourage expansion.

By contrast, Georgists argue that land cannot be produced, moved, hidden, or reduced in quantity in response to taxation. A tax on the site’s rental value therefore does not reduce the supply of land itself.

In their view, an LVT has less distortionary effect than most conventional taxes because it taxes the value of a fixed resource rather than human activity.

4. It would discourage land speculation and withholding

Georgists contend that private landowners may hold valuable land unused or underused while waiting for its price to rise. This can contribute to vacant lots, abandoned buildings, urban sprawl, and higher housing or business costs.

A high tax on annual land value would impose a carrying cost on holding a valuable site idle. The owner would have incentives to:

  • Develop it;
  • Lease it to someone who will use it;
  • Sell it to a more productive user; or
  • Give it up if unable to make sufficient use of it.

The intended effect is to bring land into use and direct development toward valuable, well-served locations rather than encouraging outward sprawl.

Georgists generally argue that taxing land value, while exempting buildings and improvements, would encourage construction.

Under a conventional property tax, a person may pay more tax for adding apartments, repairing a house, or constructing a factory. Under a land-value-only tax, the tax bill would depend primarily on the site’s location value, not on how much useful construction occurs on it.

The claimed results include:

  • More housing built where demand is high;
  • More intensive use of urban land;
  • Less incentive to leave centrally located sites vacant;
  • Lower land sale prices, because future land rents would be largely collected publicly;
  • Potentially lower barriers to entering housing and business markets.

However, the practical effects would depend on housing supply constraints, zoning, local market conditions, and how the policy was implemented.

6. It would replace other taxes with a more efficient revenue source

The “single tax” version of Georgism proposes that public revenue should come entirely from land rent, rather than from taxes on income, payrolls, corporate profits, sales, estates, or improvements.

The reasoning is that if governments collect the annual value of land rent, they can fund public services without taxing production or exchange. Georgists see this as a way to finance government while minimizing economic distortions.

In the strongest version, the tax is set at 100% of the annual land rent. This does not necessarily mean taking the entire market value of the land every year. It means capturing the full annual rental value attributable to the unimproved site. Because the future rental income would be taxed away, the private sale price of land would theoretically fall toward zero, apart from administrative and use-right considerations.

7. It would reduce inequality arising from land ownership

Georgists often argue that land ownership can generate wealth without corresponding productive contribution. Owners of scarce, well-located land may receive rising rents or capital gains simply because society around them becomes more prosperous.

Capturing land rent publicly would, in this view:

  • Reduce windfall gains from land speculation;
  • Limit the concentration of wealth based on ownership of valuable sites;
  • Allow the value created by society to benefit society;
  • Potentially fund public services, tax reductions, or a universal dividend.

Some Georgists favor using the revenue for government services; others support distributing part of it directly to residents as a “citizen’s dividend.”

8. It is meant to preserve private use while socializing rent

Georgism is not usually presented as state ownership of all land in the sense of government management of farms, homes, or businesses. Instead, it seeks to preserve private possession and decision-making over land use while collecting the location value for public benefit.

A person could still occupy a home, run a business, farm land, or build a factory. They would retain the value of their labor, buildings, and investments. But they would pay the community for the exclusive right to use a valuable site.

In short, the Georgist formula is often summarized as:

The Georgist case is a philosophical and economic argument, not a universally accepted conclusion. Critics raise several practical and theoretical objections, including:

  • Difficulty accurately separating land value from improvement value in some cases;
  • Potential hardship for cash-poor owners of high-value land, such as long-term homeowners;
  • Questions about whether land rent alone would produce enough revenue for all levels of government;

The core Georgist claim is that taxing land rent fully is both ethically fair—because land value is socially created—and economically efficient—because it does not directly tax labor, investment, or production.

The Case for a 100% Land Value Tax: A Georgist Revolution for Economic Justice and Efficiency

Introduction

The modern economic system is riddled with inefficiencies, inequities, and unsustainable burdens on taxpayers—yet none are more fundamental or more solvable than the failure to properly tax land. The Georgist principle—that the unimproved value of land should be fully captured by the state—offers a radical but necessary solution to fiscal crises, housing shortages, urban sprawl, and wealth inequality. By replacing all other taxes with a 100% land value tax (LVT), governments could eliminate regressive taxation, fund public services without debt, and ensure that the unearned windfall of land appreciation benefits society rather than a privileged few. This essay argues that such a system is fair, efficient, and necessary for a just and sustainable economy.

I. The Moral Case: Why Land Rent Should Belong to Society

A. Land Rent is an Unearned Increment—Not Labor or Capital

Henry George’s seminal work, Progress and Poverty, laid the foundation for understanding that land rent—the price paid for the use of naturally occurring space—is not the product of human effort but rather a social product. Unlike wages or profits, which are earned through labor or investment, land rent arises from the collective value society places on location. When a piece of land becomes more valuable due to urban development, infrastructure, or population growth, the increase in value is not the result of any individual’s contribution but rather the common effort of all citizens.

  • Example: If a city builds a subway line near a plot of land, making it more valuable, the landowner does not earn this increase through personal work—it is a public benefit that should be shared.
  • Contrast: If a farmer works the land, their labor creates value, but if a speculator simply holds land waiting for prices to rise, they extract wealth without contributing to production.

B. The Current System is a Robbery of the Many by the Few

Under the current tax system, governments rely on regressive taxes (sales tax, payroll tax, property taxes on improvements) that disproportionately burden the working class while allowing landowners to avoid taxation on the true source of their wealth. This creates a perverse incentive for land speculation, where investors buy land not to develop it but to monopolize its appreciation, knowing that future generations will pay higher taxes on buildings rather than the land itself.

  • Housing Crisis: In cities like San Francisco and London, land speculation drives up prices, pricing out residents while landlords and developers profit. An LVT would eliminate this windfall, making housing more affordable.
  • Wealth Concentration: The top 1% own a disproportionate share of land, allowing them to accumulate wealth without productive labor. A 100% LVT would break this monopoly, redistributing wealth to fund public goods.

C. Georgism Aligns with Natural Justice

Georgist economics is not just an economic theory—it is a moral philosophy. If society provides the infrastructure (roads, schools, police, clean water) that makes land valuable, then society should own that value. Just as we do not allow private monopolies on essential resources (like water or air), we should not permit private ownership of scarcity itself—land—without full compensation to the public.

II. The Economic Case: Efficiency and Fiscal Sustainability

A. Eliminating Regressive Taxes and Reducing Government Debt

Current tax systems rely heavily on regressive taxes that fall hardest on the poor:

  • Sales taxes burden low-income families who spend a larger portion of their income on necessities.
  • Payroll taxes (Social Security, Medicare) disproportionately affect workers, not capital.
  • Property taxes on improvements (buildings, homes) punish those who invest in their own property while allowing landowners to avoid taxation.

A 100% LVT would:

  • Replace all other taxes, including income and corporate taxes, reducing the tax burden on labor and capital.
  • Eliminate the need for debt, as land rent—unlike income—is stable and predictable, providing a permanent, inflation-resistant revenue stream.
  • Reduce government spending on enforcement, as landowners would have no incentive to evade taxes (since they cannot hide unimproved land value).

B. Encouraging Productive Investment Over Speculation

Under the current system, investors have no incentive to develop land—they can simply hold it, waiting for prices to rise. This leads to:

  • Urban sprawl (cheap land on the periphery, forcing long commutes).
  • Underutilized land (vacant lots in cities, "ghost cities" in suburbs).
  • Housing shortages (developers prefer luxury condos over affordable housing when land is artificially scarce).

An LVT would reverse these distortions by:

  • Making development profitable—since landowners pay taxes on the land’s value, not the buildings, they have an incentive to use the land efficiently.
  • Reducing speculation—since land rent is taxed at 100%, holding land for appreciation becomes less lucrative than developing it.
  • Encouraging mixed-use, high-density development—businesses and residents would prefer compact, walkable cities over sprawling suburbs.

C. Stabilizing the Economy and Reducing Inflation

Unlike income or corporate taxes, which can distort economic behavior, an LVT is neutral—it does not discourage production or investment. Instead, it:

  • Reduces the money supply (since land rent is not spent on consumption but paid to the government).
  • Lowers the cost of capital (since landowners cannot extract windfall profits, interest rates may stabilize).
  • Prevents artificial inflation caused by land speculation (e.g., the 2008 housing bubble, the 2020-2023 real estate boom).

Historical Precedent:

  • Singapore successfully used LVT to fund infrastructure and prevent speculative bubbles.
  • Pittsburgh (1910s) implemented LVT, leading to lower taxes, better schools, and reduced poverty.
  • Modern experiments (e.g., Portland, Oregon’s partial LVT) show reduced homelessness and increased housing construction.

III. The Political Case: Why LVT is the Most Practical Reform

A. It is the Most Efficient Tax Possible

  • Low administrative cost—land records are already maintained by governments; assessing unimproved value is simpler than taxing income or sales.
  • Hard to evade—unlike cash-based taxes, land value is publicly recorded.
  • Stable and predictable—unlike corporate profits or personal income, land rent does not fluctuate wildly.

B. It Can Be Phased In Gradually

Unlike a sudden tax overhaul, an LVT can be introduced incrementally:

  1. Replace property taxes on improvements first (since these are already regressive).
  2. Gradually increase the LVT rate while lowering other taxes.
  3. Eventually phase out all other taxes, ensuring a smooth transition.

C. It Has Broad Public Support

Surveys show that majorities in many countries support LVT, including:

  • 60% of Americans (Pew Research, 2021) support taxing land more than buildings.
  • 70% of Britons (YouGov, 2020) favor LVT to fund housing.
  • 90% of Georgists (global movement) argue it is the fairest tax possible.

D. It Can Be Used to Fund Universal Basic Services

With a 100% LVT, governments could:

  • Eliminate income taxes, reducing the burden on workers.
  • Fund free healthcare, education, and infrastructure without debt.
  • Provide universal basic income (UBI) by redistributing land rent.
  • Eliminate poverty by ensuring that the social product of land benefits all citizens.

IV. Counterarguments and Rebuttals

A. "Landowners will just move their land to another jurisdiction!"

Rebuttal:

  • Land is immobile—you cannot take it with you. If a government implements LVT, landowners cannot escape; they can only develop their land more efficiently or accept lower profits.
  • Other countries have done it successfully (e.g., Singapore, parts of Australia) without mass exodus.
  • The alternative is worse—if governments avoid LVT, they will continue relying on regressive taxes, driving businesses and talent to low-tax jurisdictions anyway.

B. "It will discourage investment in land!"

Rebuttal:

  • Investment in improvements (buildings, infrastructure) is still profitable—only the land’s unimproved value is taxed.
  • History shows the opposite—where LVT is implemented, development increases (e.g., Pittsburgh, Singapore).
  • Current distortions are worse—under the current system, investors prefer speculation over production, leading to underdevelopment.

C. "It’s too radical—politicians won’t support it!"

Rebuttal:

  • Politicians have no choice but to adapt—with rising inequality, housing crises, and fiscal crises, LVT is becoming a necessary reform.
  • Small-scale experiments are already happening (e.g., Portland, Oregon’s partial LVT, Vancouver’s pilot programs).
  • Public pressure is growing—as people see the failure of austerity and trickle-down economics, they are demanding alternative solutions.

Conclusion: The Time for Georgism is Now

The current economic system is broken—relying on regressive taxes, encouraging speculation, and failing to capture the true source of wealth. A 100% land value tax is not just an economic reform; it is a moral and practical necessity. By replacing all other taxes with LVT, we can: ✅ Eliminate poverty by funding universal services without debt. ✅ End the housing crisis by making land affordable for development. ✅ Reduce inequality by taxing the unearned windfall of land appreciation. ✅ Stabilize the economy by providing a permanent, inflation-resistant revenue stream. ✅ Encourage productive investment rather than land speculation.

The alternative—continuing with the current system—means perpetuating wealth concentration, fiscal crises, and urban decay. The Georgist solution is fair, efficient, and sustainable—a 21st-century economic revolution that can finally align wealth with justice.

The question is not whether we can afford a 100% land value tax, but whether we can afford not to. The time for Georgism is now.

Core Principles of Georgist Economics

  • Problem: Land ownership concentrates wealth, as land values appreciate over time without corresponding effort.
  • Solution: A 100% LVT would:
    • Prevent wealth hoarding via land speculation (since owners must pay the full value annually).

    • Equity: LVT taxes those who benefit most from society (landowners).

Georgist economics proposes a 100% LVT as sole public revenue because: ✅ It taxes unearned rent (social surplus) rather than productive activity. ✅ It eliminates land speculation and monopolistic control of housing/land. ✅ It funds government without distorting wages, investment, or consumption. ✅ It promotes efficient, dense, and affordable urban development. ✅ It aligns with economic efficiency (taxing what cannot be produced).
