Model Response:

The Single Tax on Land: Justice, Efficiency, and the Birthright of All

A Case for the Full Capture of Land Rent as Public Revenue

Introduction

In 1879, a self-taught political economist named Henry George published Progress and Poverty, a work that would become one of the best-selling books of its era and ignite a worldwide movement for economic reform. George posed a deceptively simple question: Why, amid unprecedented advances in productive technology, does poverty persist and even deepen? His answer was as elegant as it was radical — the private monopolization of land and natural resources allows a class of owners to siphon the wealth generated by society's collective progress into private rents, leaving laborers and capital with diminishing shares. His remedy was equally clear: abolish all taxes on labor and capital, and fund government entirely through a single tax equal to the full annual rental value of unimproved land.

Nearly a century and a half later, George's proposal remains not only relevant but urgent. The worldwide explosion of housing costs, the obscene concentration of wealth in the hands of those who own the most desirable locations on Earth, the persistent punishment of productive activity through income and sales taxes, and the deepening sense that the economy is rigged — all of these crises point toward the same structural flaw George identified. The land value tax (LVT), set at 100% of the unimproved rental value of land and serving as the sole source of public revenue, is not merely a policy improvement. It is a moral imperative, an economic optimization, and the foundation upon which a truly just society can be built.

This essay will argue that a full land value tax is justified on three interlocking grounds: philosophical justice, economic efficiency, and practical superiority to all existing forms of taxation. It will address common objections and demonstrate that the Georgist single tax is perhaps the most thoroughly defensible policy proposal in the history of political economy.

Part I: The Moral Case — Land Belongs to Everyone

The Nature of Land

The case for a 100% land value tax begins with a fundamental distinction that modern economics has dangerously obscured: the distinction between land and capital. Capital — buildings, machinery, tools, inventory, intellectual property — is the product of human effort. Someone built it, designed it, or organized its creation. Land, by contrast, is not produced by any human being. The surface of the Earth, the electromagnetic spectrum, mineral deposits, water rights, orbital slots, and the spatial locations upon which all human activity must take place — none of these were manufactured. They existed before any person drew breath, and they will persist long after the last of us is gone.

This distinction is not pedantic; it is the hinge upon which the entire moral argument turns. When a person builds a house, they have a natural and obvious claim to the fruits of their labor — the house itself. But the lot beneath it, the location it occupies, the proximity to roads and schools and markets — these are not the product of the owner's effort. The value of a plot of land in Manhattan versus an identical-sized plot in rural Kansas has nothing to do with anything the respective owners did. It has everything to do with the presence, activity, and investment of the surrounding community and society at large.

The Lockean Foundation and Its Limits

John Locke, often regarded as the philosophical father of private property, argued that a person gains ownership of natural resources by "mixing their labor" with them. But Locke attached a critical proviso: such appropriation is just only "where there is enough, and as good, left in common for others." This proviso is almost never satisfied in the modern world. Every square meter of desirable land on Earth is claimed. Newcomers — whether immigrants, young people, or the simply dispossessed — find that access to the Earth itself has been enclosed and priced beyond their means. They must pay rent simply to exist in a location where their labor can be productive.

This is not merely unfortunate. It is unjust by Locke's own standard. When the Lockean proviso fails, as it manifestly has, the moral basis for the private appropriation of land value collapses. What remains defensible is the private use of land — the right to occupy and improve a parcel — but not the private capture of the rent that attaches to it by virtue of communal development.

Thomas Paine and the Common Inheritance

Thomas Paine, in Agrarian Justice (1797), articulated this point with characteristic clarity. The Earth, he argued, "in its natural, uncultivated state was, and ever would have continued to be, the common property of the human race." While cultivation and improvement create private property in the products of labor, the land itself remains a common inheritance. Paine proposed a fund, financed by ground rent, to compensate every person for the loss of their natural inheritance. A 100% land value tax is simply the complete and logically consistent fulfillment of Paine's vision.

The Injustice of the Current System

Consider how the current system works in practice. A person buys a parcel of empty land near a growing city. They do absolutely nothing to it — no building, no cultivation, no improvement of any kind. Over ten years, the city grows around the parcel. Roads are built with public funds. Schools open. Businesses arrive. The population increases. The value of the parcel triples. The owner sells and pockets a windfall of hundreds of thousands — or millions — of dollars. For what? For having had enough prior wealth to hold a piece of the Earth out of use while others improved the surrounding area.

Meanwhile, a carpenter who spent those same ten years building and repairing homes — creating tangible value with her own hands — is taxed on every dollar she earns, every purchase she makes, and every structure she builds. The system, as it stands, punishes the producer and rewards the rent-seeker. It taxes effort and subsidizes idleness. No moral framework worthy of the name can defend this arrangement.

A 100% land value tax corrects this inversion. It says: what you produce is yours; what the community produces belongs to the community. It draws the line precisely where justice demands it be drawn — between earned and unearned income.

Part II: The Economic Case — Efficiency Without Distortion

The Deadweight Loss of Conventional Taxes

Every introductory economics textbook teaches that taxes on productive activity create deadweight loss — a reduction in total economic welfare caused by the distortion of incentives. Tax labor, and people work less or move their activity underground. Tax capital gains, and investors allocate resources less efficiently. Tax sales, and transactions that would have benefited both buyer and seller never occur. Tax corporate profits, and businesses engage in elaborate and socially wasteful avoidance strategies, relocate to tax havens, or simply produce less.

The scale of this deadweight loss is enormous. Economists have estimated that the marginal excess burden of income taxation in the United States ranges from 25 to 50 cents per dollar of revenue raised — meaning that for every dollar the government collects in income tax, the economy loses an additional 25 to 50 cents in foregone productive activity. The compliance costs alone — the armies of accountants, lawyers, and IRS agents devoted to navigating and enforcing the tax code — represent hundreds of billions of dollars annually in pure waste.

The Unique Efficiency of the Land Value Tax

A tax on the unimproved value of land produces zero deadweight loss. This is not a contested claim among economists; it is one of the most firmly established results in public finance theory. The reasoning is straightforward: the supply of land is perfectly inelastic. No matter how heavily you tax it, you cannot create less of it, move it offshore, or hide it in a shell corporation. A 100% tax on land rent does not reduce the quantity of land available — it merely redirects the rent from private pockets to the public treasury.

This was recognized not only by Henry George but by economists across the ideological spectrum. Milton Friedman, the patron saint of free-market economics, called the land value tax "the least bad tax." More precisely, he noted that it is the only tax that does not distort economic decisions. This is an extraordinary endorsement from a thinker whose entire career was devoted to minimizing government interference in markets.

But Friedman's phrasing was too modest. The land value tax is not merely the "least bad" tax — it is a good tax. It does not merely avoid harm; it actively improves economic outcomes.

Eliminating Land Speculation

One of the most destructive features of the current system is speculative land hoarding. Because land values tend to rise over time — driven by population growth, infrastructure investment, and economic development — landowners have a powerful incentive to hold land vacant or underutilized, waiting for its value to increase. This artificial scarcity of available land drives up rents and property prices, restricts housing supply, forces urban sprawl, lengthens commutes, increases infrastructure costs, and excludes working people from the areas where their labor is most productive.

A 100% land value tax eliminates this incentive entirely. If the full rental value of land must be paid to the public treasury regardless of whether the land is used, there is no profit in holding it idle. Speculators would rush to either develop their holdings to their highest and best use or release them to someone who will. The result would be an immediate and dramatic increase in the effective supply of well-located land, a collapse in speculative land prices, a renaissance of urban infill development, and a substantial reduction in housing costs.

This is not speculation (ironically enough). Wherever partial land value taxes have been implemented — in cities such as Harrisburg, Pennsylvania; in various Australian states; in parts of Denmark, Estonia, Singapore, and Taiwan — the results have consistently shown increased construction, reduced land speculation, and more efficient land use. A full 100% capture would magnify these benefits to their theoretical maximum.

Optimal Allocation of Resources

Under the current system, vast amounts of human ingenuity are devoted to the acquisition, trading, financing, and tax-sheltering of land and land-derived assets. Real estate speculation is the largest single category of investment in most advanced economies. The financial sector has swollen to grotesque proportions in large part because its primary function has become the capitalization and securitization of land rent — packaging future land rents into mortgage-backed securities, derivatives, and other instruments that contributed directly to the 2008 financial crisis.

A 100% land value tax would, in effect, nationalize the rental value of land while leaving land use entirely in private hands. The market would still determine who uses which parcel and for what purpose — the price mechanism would operate exactly as before. But the rents flowing to landowners would be redirected to the public, and the speculative capitalized value of land would fall to approximately zero. The trillions of dollars currently locked up in land values would become available for genuine productive investment — factories, research, infrastructure, education, entrepreneurship. The financial sector would shrink to its appropriate, utilitarian function of intermediating between savers and productive borrowers. The misallocation of talent into rent-seeking occupations — luxury real estate brokerage, speculative finance, tax law — would be corrected as those fields became less lucrative and genuinely productive work became more so.

The Henry George Theorem

In 1977, the Nobel laureate economist Joseph Stiglitz formalized what is now known as the Henry George Theorem: in an economy with optimal public goods provision, the aggregate land rent equals the aggregate expenditure on public goods. This remarkable result means that, under plausible conditions, a 100% land value tax is not merely one possible way to fund government — it is the exactly sufficient way. Public investment in infrastructure, education, security, and other public goods increases the productivity of surrounding land by precisely the amount of the investment, which is then captured back through the land value tax in a self-funding virtuous cycle.

This is one of the most beautiful results in all of economics. It means that Georgist public finance is not an arbitrary moral preference — it is the equilibrium solution to the problem of funding public goods. A government funded entirely by land rent is a government that invests exactly the right amount in public goods, because every dollar of investment is reflected in a dollar of increased land rent that funds the next dollar of investment.

Part III: Practical Advantages of the Single Tax

Simplicity and Transparency

The United States Internal Revenue Code spans over 6,500 pages. The total body of federal tax regulations, rulings, and case law fills entire libraries. American individuals and businesses spend an estimated 6 to 8 billion hours annually on tax compliance. The tax preparation industry alone is worth over $14 billion per year. This colossal apparatus of bureaucratic complexity exists because the current system attempts to tax things that are inherently difficult to measure and easy to conceal — income, profits, sales, gifts, estates.

Land, by contrast, cannot be hidden, moved, or misrepresented. It sits in plain sight. Every parcel is surveyed, mapped, and recorded. Modern geographic information systems, satellite imagery, and statistical modeling make it possible to assess unimproved land values with a high degree of accuracy and at minimal cost. A land value tax would reduce the entire apparatus of tax collection to a simple, transparent, and nearly unevadable system: assess the rental value of each parcel, send the bill, and collect. The IRS as we know it could be largely dismantled. Tax attorneys and accountants could redirect their considerable talents to productive purposes. The cognitive burden on every citizen of understanding, calculating, and complying with a labyrinthine tax code would vanish.

Elimination of Tax Avoidance and Evasion

Tax avoidance — the legal manipulation of the tax code to reduce liability — and tax evasion — the illegal concealment of taxable activity — are among the most corrosive forces in modern economies. They erode the tax base, shift the burden onto honest taxpayers, breed cynicism about the fairness of the system, and divert enormous resources into socially unproductive activity.

A land value tax is essentially immune to both avoidance and evasion. You cannot move land to the Cayman Islands. You cannot reclassify it as a different kind of asset. You cannot employ a team of lawyers to find loopholes in a tax that is levied on a single, physically observable, publicly recorded quantity. You cannot underreport your land, because public records and market evidence establish its value independently of any declaration by the owner. The simplicity and inevitability of the tax would restore public confidence in the fairness of the revenue system — a benefit whose value is incalculable.

Progressivity Without Bureaucracy

Critics of flat taxes often object that they are regressive — placing a proportionally greater burden on lower-income households. A land value tax, while technically a flat rate on land value, is inherently progressive in its economic incidence. This is because land ownership is far more concentrated than income. The wealthiest households and corporations own vastly disproportionate shares of land value, particularly the most valuable urban and commercial land. A 100% land value tax would effectively constitute a massive transfer from the wealthiest members of society — those whose wealth is most heavily derived from the passive ownership of appreciating land — to the general public.

At the same time, it would unburden the working poor and middle class, who currently pay income taxes, payroll taxes, sales taxes, and property taxes on their improvements (the buildings they live in), while holding relatively little land value. Under a Georgist system, a family renting an apartment would pay no taxes at all. A family owning a modest home on a small lot would see their tax burden shift from income and building value to the much smaller land value beneath their home — almost certainly a net reduction. The only people who would pay substantially more are those who own large amounts of valuable land — precisely the people whose wealth is most thoroughly unearned.

Ending the Housing Crisis

The global housing affordability crisis is, at root, a land crisis. In every major city where housing is unaffordable — San Francisco, London, Sydney, Vancouver, Hong Kong — the cost of the structure itself is a small fraction of the total price. What is expensive is the land. And the land is expensive because its value is allowed to be privately captured and speculated upon, creating a self-reinforcing cycle in which rising prices attract more speculation, further restricting supply and driving prices higher.

A 100% land value tax would break this cycle decisively. By taxing away the full rental value of land, it would reduce the purchase price of land to approximately zero — since an asset whose entire return is taxed away has no capitalized market value. Housing would cost only what it costs to build, maintain, and finance the physical structure. In most markets, this would represent a reduction in housing costs of 50% or more. Homeownership would become accessible to millions of people currently priced out. The obscenity of working families paying 40%, 50%, or 60% of their income simply for a place to live would be consigned to history.

Promoting Genuine Free Markets

There is a deep irony in the current economic order: those who most loudly champion "free markets" are often the most vigorous defenders of the institution that distorts markets most severely — private land rent. A market in which access to the Earth itself is monopolized by a fraction of the population is not a free market. It is a market distorted at its foundation by an artificial scarcity of the most basic factor of production.

The Georgist single tax would create genuinely free markets in the fullest sense. Labor would be untaxed, free to command its full market wage. Capital would be untaxed, free to earn its full market return. Entrepreneurship would be untaxed, free to capture the full reward for innovation and risk. The only thing taxed would be the monopoly return on a resource no one created — a return that exists only because society has collectively made certain locations more productive than others. Far from being anti-market, the single tax would remove the single largest market distortion in the modern economy and unleash competitive forces that are currently suppressed by the tribute extracted by landowners.

Part IV: Addressing Objections

"But I paid for my land!"

This is perhaps the most emotionally compelling objection, and it deserves a serious response. Yes, many current landowners purchased their land at market prices, often investing their life savings. A sudden imposition of a 100% land value tax would dramatically reduce the market value of their asset, potentially causing severe financial hardship.

This is a legitimate concern about transition, not about the justice or efficiency of the tax itself. Several approaches can address it. First, the tax can be phased in gradually — increasing by a few percentage points per year over two or three decades, giving landowners ample time to adjust. Second, revenue from the land value tax can be partially distributed as a citizens' dividend — a universal payment to every resident — which would compensate most homeowners for their loss in land value. Third, we must recognize that the "loss" experienced by current landowners is not the destruction of real wealth but the deflation of a speculative bubble — the same kind of deflation that occurs when any unjust privilege is revoked. The slaveholder in 1865 "paid for" his slaves. That did not make abolition unjust. The holder of a taxi medallion "paid for" his monopoly privilege. That did not make deregulation wrong. The current price of land reflects the capitalized present value of all expected future rents — rents that, as we have argued, are morally the property of the community. Phasing in the recapture of those rents, with appropriate transitional measures, is not a taking. It is a long-overdue correction.

"Land values cannot be accurately assessed."

On the contrary, the assessment of unimproved land values is far easier than the assessment of structures, incomes, or business profits. Land values are determined by location, and location values are revealed continuously by market transactions. Modern mass appraisal techniques, combined with geographic information systems and statistical modeling, can estimate unimproved site values with a high degree of accuracy. Many jurisdictions already perform such assessments for existing property tax purposes. Moreover, the incentive structure under a land value tax encourages honest assessment: since the tax captures the full rental value, there is no incentive to overassess (which would cause land to be abandoned to the public) or underassess (which would be detected by comparison with market evidence). Assessment disputes, while not eliminated, would be simpler and less consequential than the vast web of disputes, audits, and litigation generated by the income tax.

"Land rent is not sufficient to fund government."

This empirical objection deserves careful examination. Estimates of total land rent in the United States vary, but serious studies — including those by economists such as Mason Gaffney, Fred Harrison, and researchers at the Lincoln Institute of Land Policy — suggest that total land rent (including rent from natural resources and the electromagnetic spectrum) is in the range of 20% to 35% of GDP. Federal, state, and local government spending in the United States is approximately 35% to 40% of GDP.

At first glance, there appears to be a shortfall. But several factors close the gap. First, current land rents are depressed by the existing tax system, which taxes improvements and thereby reduces the residual rent attributable to land. Removing taxes on improvements and labor would dramatically increase land rents, as the full productivity of each site would be reflected in its rental value. Second, a huge portion of current government spending is devoted to programs made necessary by the distortions of the current system — welfare programs to compensate for poverty caused by land monopoly, infrastructure subsidies driven by sprawl caused by land speculation, military spending to secure access to foreign natural resources. Under a Georgist system, many of these expenditures would be reduced or eliminated. Third, a citizens' dividend funded by land rent would replace much of the existing welfare state, simplifying administration and reducing overhead. The Henry George Theorem provides the theoretical basis for believing that, in a well-functioning economy, land rent is precisely sufficient to fund optimal public goods provision.

"This would destroy the real estate industry."

It would radically transform it, and for the better. The real estate industry, as currently constituted, is largely an apparatus for the trading and financing of land values — values that, under a Georgist system, would approach zero. But the demand for actual real estate services — construction, renovation, property management, brokerage of structures — would remain robust and likely grow, as the elimination of taxes on improvements would stimulate a construction boom. What would disappear is the parasitic speculation in land values that inflates the industry beyond its productive function and periodically triggers devastating financial crises.

"What about farmers and rural landowners?"

Agricultural land has relatively low value compared to urban and commercial land. The overwhelming majority of land value is concentrated in cities. A 100% land value tax would be a light burden on rural landowners and a heavy burden on owners of prime urban real estate — exactly the incidence that justice and efficiency demand. Moreover, farmers who actively cultivate their land are currently doubly burdened — they pay property taxes on their improvements (barns, irrigation systems, fences) and income taxes on their earnings. Under a Georgist system, they would pay only the land value tax on the unimproved value of their acreage, which in most rural areas is modest. Most working farmers would see a substantial net reduction in their total tax burden.

Part V: The Moral Urgency of the Present Moment

We live in an era defined by a paradox: technological productivity has never been higher, yet broad-based prosperity feels increasingly out of reach. Housing costs consume ever-larger shares of household income. Wealth inequality has reached levels not seen since the Gilded Age. Young people face the prospect of being permanently locked out of homeownership. The tax code rewards financial engineering and punishes honest labor. The financial system periodically implodes under the weight of speculative bubbles built on the capitalized value of land.

All of these pathologies trace back to the same structural cause that Henry George identified in 1879: the private monopolization of land rent. And all of them have the same structural solution.

The beauty of the Georgist single tax is that it does not require us to choose between equity and efficiency, between justice and growth, between freedom and fairness. It delivers all of these simultaneously. It is the rare policy that satisfies libertarian, progressive, and utilitarian moral frameworks alike. It rewards producers and penalizes rent-seekers. It funds public goods without distorting private choices. It breaks up concentrated wealth without confiscating the fruits of anyone's labor. It makes housing affordable without price controls. It promotes environmental stewardship by putting a price on the occupation of nature. It simplifies government without reducing its capacity. It is, in short, as close to a free lunch as economics ever offers — and economics, as we are often reminded, is the science of the non-existence of free lunches.

Conclusion

The case for a 100% land value tax as the sole source of public revenue rests on three pillars, each independently compelling and together overwhelming:

First, it is just. The value of land is created by nature and by community, not by individual effort. To allow private individuals to capture this value is to permit the enclosure of a common inheritance — a form of privilege indistinguishable in principle from feudal land grants or the ownership of human beings. What a person produces belongs to that person. What the community produces belongs to the community.

Second, it is efficient. Unlike every other tax, the land value tax creates zero deadweight loss, eliminates speculation, promotes the optimal use of land, and removes the enormous compliance and distortionary costs of the existing tax system. It is the only tax that leading economists from Adam Smith to Milton Friedman to Joseph Stiglitz have endorsed as non-distortionary.

Third, it is practical. Land cannot be hidden, moved, or disguised. Assessment is straightforward. Collection is simple. Avoidance is impossible. The administrative apparatus required is a fraction of what the current system demands.

Henry George wrote, "The equal right of all men to the use of land is as clear as their equal right to breathe the air — it is a right proclaimed by the fact of their existence." For too long, we have organized our economies around the denial of this right. We have taxed the worker and freed the landlord. We have punished production and rewarded monopoly. We have treated the Earth as the private property of those fortunate enough to have enclosed it, and demanded tribute from those who merely wish to live and labor upon it.

It is time — long past time — to reverse this. It is time to recognize that the rent of land belongs to all of us, that its full capture for public benefit is the foundation of a just and prosperous society, and that the single tax is not a utopian dream but a practical, proven, and profoundly moral policy whose implementation would represent the greatest advance in economic justice since the abolition of slavery.

The Earth belongs to everyone. Let us build our public institutions on that truth.

"Men did not make the earth. It is the value of the improvements only, and not the earth itself, that is individual property. Every proprietor owes to the community a ground-rent for the land which he holds." — Thomas Paine, Agrarian Justice, 1797

Georgist Land Value Tax: Claimed Benefits and Rationale

Background

Henry George, in his 1879 work Progress and Poverty, argued that a tax on the unimproved value of land — sometimes called the "Single Tax" — should replace all other taxes. The philosophy rests on several interconnected claims.

Moral and Philosophical Foundation

Land as distinct from capital: Georgists draw a sharp distinction between land (natural resources and locations no one created) and capital (buildings, machines, and other things people produce). They argue that because no individual created land, the value arising from its scarcity and location is a product of the community rather than the landowner's effort.

The problem of rent: When a community grows, builds infrastructure, or improves services, nearby land values rise. Georgists argue that private landowners capture this value — which they call "economic rent" — without contributing to its creation. George characterized this as a fundamental injustice allowing passive enrichment at collective expense.

Equal claim to nature: Georgists often invoke a natural rights argument: every person has an equal claim to the earth's natural opportunities. Allowing private collection of land rent effectively charges others for access to what should be a common inheritance.

Economic Efficiency Arguments

Non-distortionary taxation: This is perhaps the most recognized economic claim. Because the supply of land is fixed — no one can manufacture more land in a given location — Georgists argue that taxing its unimproved value does not reduce the quantity available or discourage its production. In standard economic terms, the supply curve is perfectly inelastic, so the tax theoretically creates no deadweight loss. This argument has received support from economists across various traditions, including Milton Friedman, who called it "the least bad tax."

Eliminating harmful taxes: By replacing income taxes, sales taxes, payroll taxes, and capital gains taxes, Georgists argue you remove disincentives to work, save, invest, trade, and build. The claim is that current tax systems punish productive activity, whereas a land value tax would not.

Discouraging speculation and promoting efficient use: A 100% tax on unimproved land value would make it costly to hold land idle or underused while waiting for appreciation. Georgists argue this would:

  • Push vacant and underutilized land into productive use
  • Reduce speculative land bubbles
  • Lower the barrier to entry for those who want to use land productively
  • Encourage denser, more efficient development in areas with high land values

Breaking land monopoly: George argued that concentrated land ownership functions as a monopoly on access to natural opportunities, allowing landowners to extract rent from laborers and capital-holders. Taxing away this rent would, in theory, redirect economic rewards toward labor and productive investment.

Claimed Macroeconomic Benefits

Resolving the paradox of progress and poverty: George's central puzzle was why poverty persists alongside economic advancement. His answer was that gains from progress are absorbed into rising land rents rather than distributed as higher wages or returns to capital. Capturing land rent publicly would, he argued, allow prosperity to be more broadly shared.

Reducing inequality: Since land ownership is typically concentrated among the wealthy, and since land value represents a significant share of total wealth, Georgists argue the tax would substantially reduce wealth inequality without discouraging productive economic activity.

Stabilizing business cycles: Some Georgists, notably Fred Harrison, argue that speculative land booms and busts are a primary driver of economic cycles. By removing the incentive for speculation, the tax would theoretically dampen these cycles.

Practical and Administrative Arguments

Difficult to evade: Land cannot be hidden, moved offshore, or concealed in shell companies. Its value in a given location is relatively transparent compared to income or financial assets. Georgists argue this makes it an administratively efficient tax base.

Simplification: Replacing a complex web of taxes with a single levy would, they claim, dramatically reduce compliance costs, bureaucratic overhead, and opportunities for avoidance.

The "Single Tax" Claim

Georgists argue that the total unimproved land rent in a modern economy is sufficient — or nearly sufficient — to fund public expenditure, making other taxes unnecessary. George himself believed it would be more than sufficient, and that the resulting economic growth from eliminating other taxes would further expand the base.

Important Caveats

These are the arguments as Georgists present them. Critics and skeptics raise several objections, including:

  • Practical difficulty in separating land value from improvement value

The Earth Belongs to Everyone: A Case for the Land Value Tax

Friends, fellow citizens, believers in justice—

I stand before you today to speak about something so fundamental, so elemental, that it hides in plain sight beneath our very feet.

The land.

Not the buildings upon it. Not the crops sown into it. Not the bridges, the roads, the factories, or the homes built by the sweat of human labor. I am talking about the land itself—the surface of the Earth, which no human being created, which no human being can replicate, and which every human being requires simply to exist.

And I am here to tell you that the way we treat land—who claims it, who profits from it, and who is excluded from it—is the single greatest source of injustice in our economy. It is the hidden engine of inequality. It is the silent tax on the productive. It is the unearned windfall of the privileged. And it is fixable.

I am here to advocate for a single, elegant, moral reform: fund our government entirely through a tax on the unimproved value of land, and abolish every other tax that punishes human effort.

I. The Problem We Refuse to See

Let me ask you a question. When a new subway line is built in a city—paid for by taxpayers—what happens to the land around the new stations? The value skyrockets. Property owners who did absolutely nothing, who laid not a single rail, who drove not a single rivet, wake up wealthier than they were the day before.

Who created that value? You did. The community did. The taxpayers did. The workers who built the line did. And yet the profit—the increase in land value—flows directly into private pockets.

This is not an exception. This is the rule.

Every road we build, every school we fund, every park we plant, every police officer we employ, every hospital we establish—all of it pours value into the land around it. And all of that value is captured not by the people who created it, but by those who simply hold title to the earth beneath it.

Henry George called this the great injustice of civilization, and he was right. In his masterwork Progress and Poverty, published in 1879—a book that sold more copies in its time than any book in the English language save the Bible—he identified a paradox that still haunts us today:

Why does poverty deepen alongside progress?

Why, in our most advanced cities, surrounded by the greatest wealth humanity has ever produced, do people sleep in doorways? Why do nurses and teachers and firefighters commute two hours because they cannot afford to live in the communities they serve? Why does a young family, with two working parents, find that the price of a modest home consumes the labor of a lifetime?

The answer is land.

As economies grow, as populations increase, as communities invest in infrastructure and culture and safety—the value of land rises. And because we allow that value to be privately captured, the fruits of collective progress are funneled to landowners, while everyone else runs faster and faster just to stay in place.

II. The Moral Case

Let us be absolutely clear about something. Land is not wealth that someone created. It is not like a chair built by a carpenter, or a novel written by an author, or a meal prepared by a chef. Those things are the products of human labor, human ingenuity, human effort. They belong rightfully to those who made them.

But the land? The land was here before us. It will be here after us. No one made Manhattan Island. No one manufactured the San Francisco Bay. No one produced the rich soil of Iowa or the oil reserves of Texas.

When someone "owns" land, what do they actually own? They own an exclusive right to occupy a portion of the Earth—a right enforced by the power of the state, backed by the implicit threat of force. Every other human being on the planet is excluded from that space.

Now—I am not saying people shouldn't have secure access to land. Of course they should! Homes should be secure. Farms should be secure. Businesses should be secure. A land value tax does not change that. You would still hold your land. You would still live in your home. You would still use your property as you see fit.

But I am saying this: the rental value of that exclusive access—the premium that location and community confer—belongs to all of us. It is the common inheritance of humanity. It is created by society, and it should be returned to society.

Thomas Paine understood this when he wrote in Agrarian Justice that every proprietor of land "owes to the community a ground-rent for the land which he holds." Thomas Jefferson understood it. John Stuart Mill understood it. Even Milton Friedman—no radical, no socialist—called the land value tax "the least bad tax."

This is not a left-wing idea. This is not a right-wing idea. This is a moral idea. It says simply: you deserve what you create, and you owe what you didn't.

III. The Economic Case

Now let me speak to those of you who care about efficiency—and you should, because inefficiency is just another word for waste, and waste means human suffering that didn't need to happen.

Our current tax system is an abomination of perverse incentives.

We tax income—and thereby punish people for working. We tax sales—and thereby punish people for buying and selling. We tax capital gains—and thereby punish people for investing. We tax corporations—and thereby punish people for building enterprises that employ their neighbors.

Every single one of these taxes creates what economists call deadweight loss—economic activity that would have happened but didn't because the tax made it unprofitable. Every one of these taxes requires a Byzantine apparatus of enforcement, a labyrinth of loopholes, an army of accountants and attorneys whose considerable talents are devoted not to producing anything of value, but to navigating a system of artificial complexity.

And what do we get in return? A system where the most productive members of society—workers, entrepreneurs, inventors, creators—bear the heaviest burden, while those who simply own and wait are rewarded.

A land value tax has zero deadweight loss. Zero.

Why? Because land is fixed in supply. You cannot make more of it. You cannot hide it in an offshore account. You cannot move it to the Cayman Islands. You cannot disguise it with creative bookkeeping. It just sits there, and its value is publicly assessable.

When you tax labor, you get less labor. When you tax investment, you get less investment. When you tax land value, you get exactly the same amount of land. The tax does not reduce the supply of land by a single square inch. It does not discourage the use of land—in fact, it does the opposite.

Here is the beautiful mechanism: A land value tax makes it expensive to hold valuable land idle. That vacant lot in downtown, held by a speculator waiting for prices to rise while the city rots around it? Under a land value tax, that speculator faces a cost for hoarding that land. They must either put it to productive use or release it to someone who will.

Speculation collapses. Land prices fall. Housing becomes affordable. Businesses can afford to open. The economy breathes.

This is not theory. We have evidence. Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, shifted toward a split-rate tax that taxed land more heavily than buildings. The result? A construction boom. Vacant properties declined by over 80 percent. The city, once listed among America's most distressed, came back to life.

Denmark, Estonia, Singapore, Hong Kong, Taiwan—places that have leaned into land value capture have seen economic dynamism that puts their peers to shame.

The land value tax doesn't just fund government. It makes the economy work better.

IV. The Simplicity

I want you to imagine something for a moment. Imagine a world where there is no income tax. No payroll tax. No sales tax. No capital gains tax. No corporate tax. No estate tax. No tax on your savings. No tax on your labor. No tax on your creativity.

Imagine April 15th means nothing to you. Imagine no withholding from your paycheck. Imagine starting a business without worrying about the tax implications of every decision. Imagine the IRS—as we know it—ceasing to exist.

Imagine instead a single, transparent, unavoidable assessment: What is the unimproved value of the land you occupy? Assessed publicly, paid regularly, and that's it.

Every dollar you earn from your labor? Yours. Every return on your investment? Yours. Every gain from your ingenuity, your risk-taking, your late nights and early mornings? Yours.

The only thing that is not yours is the thing you never created in the first place—the premium value of location, generated by the community around you.

This is not utopian fantasy. The economics work. Multiple studies—from the Lincoln Institute of Land Policy to academic economists across the world—have confirmed that the total rental value of land in advanced economies is more than sufficient to fund government at current levels. In the United States alone, estimates of aggregate land rent range from $5 trillion upward annually—a figure that comfortably exceeds total government revenue at all levels.

We do not need to dream of new revenue. We merely need to stop ignoring the revenue that is already there, flowing silently into private hands.

V. Answering the Objections

Now, I know some of you are thinking: What about the homeowner? What about the family that bought their house, paid their mortgage, and now you want to tax their land?

I hear you. And I want to address this directly, because this concern is legitimate and it deserves a serious answer.

First: under a land value tax, the building—every improvement, every renovation, every addition—is untaxed. Many homeowners would see their total tax bill decrease, because their home's value is primarily in the structure, not the land beneath it. It is prime location holders—owners of the most valuable land in the most desirable areas—who would see the greatest increase.

Second: we are not proposing to flip a switch overnight. Transition matters. A phased implementation over ten, fifteen, even twenty years—gradually shifting the tax burden from labor and enterprise onto land values—would allow markets to adjust, allow homeowners to plan, and allow the benefits to emerge organically.

Third—and perhaps most importantly—consider what homeowners gain. No income tax. No payroll tax. No sales tax. For the vast majority of homeowners, especially those outside of hyper-inflated land markets, the elimination of all other taxes would more than compensate for the land value tax. They would keep more of what they earn. Their purchasing power would increase. The economy around them would grow.

And for those who would be genuinely burdened—elderly homeowners on fixed incomes in areas where land values have soared, for example—deferral mechanisms are simple and well-established. The tax can be deferred as a lien, payable upon sale or transfer. No one is forced from their home.

But what about farmers? Farmland in rural areas has relatively low unimproved land value precisely because it is far from urban centers. The land value tax falls most heavily on urban land, where community investment has created the greatest premiums. Most farmers would see a dramatic reduction in their total tax burden.

But is there really enough revenue? Yes. Land rents are enormous—they are simply invisible because we have chosen not to measure what we have chosen not to tax. When you consider not just the surface rental value of land but also the value of natural resources, the electromagnetic spectrum, mineral rights, and other common assets, the revenue base is vast.

VI. The Justice of It

Let me bring this home. Because ultimately, this is not about economics. It is not about efficiency, though the efficiency gains are extraordinary. It is not about simplicity, though the simplicity is breathtaking.

It is about justice.

It is about a child born in a poor neighborhood whose life prospects are diminished—not because she lacks talent, not because she lacks determination, but because the land around her has been stripped of value by disinvestment while land elsewhere has been inflated by privilege.

It is about a young man who works sixty hours a week and cannot afford an apartment in the city where he works, because the land beneath that apartment building is priced to benefit an owner who contributes nothing but a deed.

It is about the fundamental question that every society must answer: Who is the Earth for?

Is it for all of us? Or is it for those who got there first, or those who could pay the most, or those who inherited the right?

Henry George answered that question 145 years ago with a clarity that still rings true:

> "We must make land common property."

Not by seizing it. Not by collectivizing it. Not by abolishing ownership. But by recognizing that the value of land—the rent of the Earth—is a common fund, belonging to every man, woman, and child, and that taxing it fully is simply a matter of returning to the people what already belongs to the people.

VII. The Call

I know this idea sounds radical. I know that in a political landscape defined by tribal warfare and incremental tinkering, the notion of replacing our entire tax system with a single, just, and efficient levy sounds impossibly ambitious.

But let me remind you: every great reform in history sounded impossible until it wasn't. The abolition of slavery. Universal suffrage. The end of child labor. These were radical ideas, championed by passionate minorities, resisted by entrenched interests, dismissed by respectable opinion—until the sheer moral force of the argument became undeniable.

The land value tax has been endorsed, in varying degrees, by Adam Smith, David Ricardo, John Stuart Mill, Leo Tolstoy, Winston Churchill, Sun Yat-sen, Albert Einstein, and Milton Friedman. It crosses every ideological boundary because it speaks to something deeper than ideology. It speaks to fairness.

Winston Churchill said it best, in a speech to Parliament in 1909:

> "Roads are made, streets are made, services are improved, electric light turns night into day, water is brought from reservoirs a hundred miles off in the mountains—and all the while the landlord sits still. Every one of those improvements is effected by the labor and cost of other people and the taxpayers. To not one of those improvements does the land monopolist, as a land monopolist, contribute, and yet by every one of them the value of his land is enhanced."

That was 1909. It is now 2024, and we are still tolerating this absurdity.

How much longer?

How much longer will we tax the nurse for healing, the teacher for teaching, the builder for building—while the mere holder of land titles collects the wealth that all of them create?

How much longer will we accept a system where the reward for labor is taxation and the reward for ownership is appreciation?

How much longer will we allow the Earth itself—the common inheritance of all mankind—to be enclosed, hoarded, and speculated upon while millions scramble for scraps?

I say: not one day longer than we must.

The path is clear. The economics are sound. The morality is unassailable. The evidence is mounting. What we lack is not knowledge. What we lack is not a plan.

What we lack is will.

So I am asking you—not for your agreement alone, but for your voice. Study this idea. Challenge it. Interrogate it. Test it against every objection you can find. I am confident—as Henry George was confident, as economists across a century and a half have been confident—that it will withstand every challenge.

And then demand it. Demand it of your city councils. Demand it of your state legislatures. Demand it of your representatives in Congress. Demand a tax system that rewards creation and reclaims extraction. Demand an economy where progress lifts everyone, not just those who hold the deeds.

The Earth belongs to all of us. It is time our tax system reflected that truth.

Thank you.

"The equal right of all men to the use of land is as clear as their equal right to breathe the air—it is a right proclaimed by the fact of their existence." — Henry George, Progress and Poverty, 1879

Title: A Case for 100% Land Value Tax: A Georgist Pathway to Fairness and Economic Efficiency

Introduction
In an era marked by widening inequality, inefficient tax systems, and unsustainable land use, the principles of Henry George, a 19th-century economist, offer a visionary solution: a 100% land value tax (LVT) on the unimproved value of land. This essay argues that capturing land rent—the value derived from land itself, independent of buildings or improvements—for public benefit is not only fair but also economically superior to existing tax models. By replacing all other taxes with a single LVT, society can achieve equity, efficiency, and sustainability, aligning economic incentives with the common good.

The Moral Imperative: Fairness Through Community Value Capture
Land, by its very nature, is a communal asset. Its value is not created by individual effort but by factors such as location, natural resources, and societal development (e.g., infrastructure, public services, and community vitality). As George articulated in Progress and Poverty, this unimproved land value is a "common-wealth" that ought to be shared by all. Taxing it does not penalize productivity, as land exists regardless of human toil. Instead, it rectifies a moral wrong: the privatization of wealth generated collectively. For instance, a plot in a bustling city center gains value not because its owner improved it but because of public investments in transit, safety, and amenities. A 100% LVT ensures that such gains are returned to the community, fostering social equity and rectifying systemic disparities in wealth accumulation.

Economic Efficiency: Eliminating Distortions and Incentivizing Productivity
Traditional taxes—on income, labor, or capital—create "deadweight loss," discouraging productive activities. Income taxes reduce incentives to work; capital taxes stifle investment. In contrast, LVT is a "natural tax" that does not distort economic behavior. Since land cannot be created or destroyed, taxing its unimproved value does not deter productive use. Rather, it encourages efficiency: landowners are motivated to develop or sell underutilized parcels to generate revenue, reducing speculation and ghost cities. Economists like Milton Friedman acknowledged LVT’s efficiency, noting its minimal impact on economic decisions. For example, cities like Pittsburgh, which adopted LVT in the early 20th century, saw reduced vacancy rates and more vibrant urban development compared to tax systems favoring improvements.

Simplification and Public Benefit: The Sole Revenue Source
Replacing all taxes with a single LVT streamlines governance. Current systems require bureaucracies to collect income, sales, and property taxes, creating administrative bloat and compliance costs. A unified LVT eliminates these inefficiencies, directing all public revenue from land rent. This system also prevents tax evasion, as land cannot be concealed or relocated. Moreover, coupling LVT with the abolition of other taxes liberates individuals and businesses from punitive levies on labor and capital, spurring innovation and equitable growth. Public services funded by LVT—schools, healthcare, infrastructure—could be more transparent and directly linked to community-driven value creation.

Addressing Counterarguments
Critics may argue that LVT burdens landowners, particularly farmers or homeowners. However, the tax targets unimproved value, not the efforts of those who improve land. A farmer’s productivity lies in crops and labor, not the soil’s innate fertility. Similarly, homeowners retain the value of their buildings. Others question feasibility, but historical precedents—such as Taiwan’s LVT-based revenue model or the success of land taxation in Scandinavia—demonstrate practicality. Transition challenges exist, but phased implementation and valuations based on land’s economic potential (a well-established practice) can mitigate disruptions.

Environmental and Social Justice Benefits
LVT also promotes sustainability. By penalizing land hoarding, it encourages higher-density development and brownfield reuse, curbing urban sprawl and habitat destruction. Socially, it addresses root causes of inequality. Unlike wealth taxes that target capital mobility, land’s immobility makes it an ideal tax base. This ensures the affluent, who disproportionately hold land, contribute their fair share. Furthermore, a 100% LVT fosters local resilience, as communities reinvest land rent into public goods that enhance their own environments.

Conclusion
A 100% land value tax is the cornerstone of a just and efficient economic system. It aligns moral principles with practical benefits: capturing the community’s shared value, eliminating distortions from other taxes, and fostering equitable growth. By embracing Georgist principles, societies can transform land from a privilege into a sustainable resource for the common good. In doing so, they pave the way for a world where prosperity is not monopolized by landowners but shared by all who contribute to economic life. The path to progress lies not in taxing labor or innovation but in valuing the land we all share.

Model Response:

For more than a century, economists from Adam Smith to Milton Friedman have agreed on one paradoxical truth: there is one perfect tax. It does not punish work, it does not punish investment, it does not punish thrift or innovation. It simply returns to the public what the public creates. That tax is a 100% tax on the unimproved value of land - the Land Value Tax, or LVT, as proposed by Henry George.

It is time we implemented it fully, and let it replace every other tax.

1. What Land Value Tax Is - and Is Not

To understand the case for LVT, you must understand what land really is in economic terms.

When economists say "land," they do not mean dirt. They mean location. They mean the unimproved value of a site: its proximity to a city center, to a harbor, to a transit stop, to good schools, to a thriving market. They mean the natural resources under it and the legal privilege to exclude others from that spot on earth.

LVT does not tax what you build. Your house, your factory, your barn, your apartment tower, your solar panels, your drainage improvements - none of that is taxed. Only the underlying location value is taxed.

If two identical lots sit side by side on the same block, they pay the same tax, even if one holds a vacant lot choked with weeds and the other holds a six-story apartment building. That distinction is the key to everything.

2. It Is Fair Because Land Value Is Created By All of Us

When a carpenter builds a chair, the value of that chair comes from his labor. When a farmer grows wheat, the value comes from his work. Taxing that value is taxing human effort.

When the value of a plot of land in Manhattan goes from $1,000 in 1800 to $100 million today, who created that value? Not the owner. He did not move the rivers, build the subway system, found the universities, build the theaters, and bring 8 million neighbors together.

That value was created by three things:

1. Nature, which no man produced. 2. The community, whose presence, commerce, roads, schools, police, and culture make a location desirable. 3. Public investment, paid for by taxpayers, that directly inflates surrounding land prices - every time a new metro station opens, nearby landowners become millionaires overnight without lifting a finger.

Under our current system we privatize that socially-created value and then socialize the costs. We allow a landowner to sit idle on a vacant downtown lot, watching its value soar as the city grows around it, while taxing the wages of the workers who actually created that growth.

A 100% LVT simply says: what the community creates, the community should collect. What the individual creates, the individual should keep in full. That is the essence of justice.

John Locke said a man has a right to what he mixes his labor with. No man ever mixed his labor with the location of Manhattan itself.

3. It Is Efficient Because It Cannot Be Avoided and Does Not Distort

Every other tax is a penalty on something good, and therefore makes less of it happen. Tax income, you get less work and more tax evasion. Tax sales, you get less commerce. Tax buildings, you get fewer buildings and more urban blight. Tax capital gains, you get less investment.

This is called deadweight loss, and economists agree it costs the United States hundreds of billions of dollars per year in lost growth.

Land is different. The amount of land on Earth is fixed. You cannot hide it in a Cayman Islands account. You cannot move it to Singapore. You cannot make less of it because it is taxed. As Milton Friedman, no radical leftist, put it: "The least bad tax is the property tax on the unimproved value of land."

If you tax a downtown parking lot at 100% of its location rent, what happens? The owner cannot raise his price - the market already determines land rent. He has three choices: develop it to generate income to pay the tax, sell it to someone who will, or surrender it. In every case, the community wins.

Under income and building taxes, owners are incentivized to keep land vacant or underused. This is why every major American city has seas of surface parking and boarded-up lots in the center while sprawl consumes farmland at the edge. LVT reverses that incentive. It makes speculation unprofitable and productive use necessary. It makes housing cheaper by bringing idle land into use, reducing sprawl, and eliminating land price bubbles.

A 100% LVT would pop real estate bubbles permanently, because there would be no profit in buying land simply to wait for the price to rise.

4. It Is sufficient To Be The Sole Source of Revenue

Henry George's central insight in Progress and Poverty (1879) was not just that LVT is fair and efficient, but that it is enough.

Land rent is enormous. Every dollar spent on rent for location - for an apartment in a good district, for retail space on a busy street, for farmland with good soil and access - is a measure of that value. In the United States alone, the total unimproved value of all land is estimated at $20-30 trillion. The annual rental value of that land is easily $2-3 trillion, roughly equal to total federal tax revenue.

And that figure grows automatically as society becomes more productive, without any increase in the tax rate. When the economy booms, land values rise, and public revenue rises with it - not by taxing workers more, but by collecting more of the socially-created surplus.

Imagine what happens when we abolish all other taxes:

No income tax: workers keep 100% of their paychecks. No penalty for earning more, working overtime, or starting a business.

No sales tax: every purchase becomes 10-30% cheaper, with the greatest benefit to the poor.

No property tax on improvements: you can renovate your home, build a second unit, start a workshop in your garage, and your tax bill does not go up by a cent.

No corporate income tax, no capital gains tax, no payroll tax: the United States would instantly become the most attractive place on earth to invest, build, and hire.

One tax. Collected once a year. Impossible to evade. Based on public assessment of publicly available land values. No IRS auditing waitresses' tips. No 70,000 pages of tax code. No loopholes for billionaires, because billionaires cannot hide land.

The Objection, Answered

The most common objection is: what about a retired widow on a valuable lot who cannot afford the tax?

The answer is practical and principled. First, under current property taxes she is already losing. LVT would typically lower taxes for the vast majority of homeowners, because most homeowners own a small piece of land but a valuable house. The current system taxes the house; LVT would not. Only owners of highly valuable land relative to their improvements - downtown lot owners, large vacant lot holders - would pay more.

Second, for that widow, payment can be deferred until sale or inheritance, with interest. She would still be far better off than under income and sales taxes she pays every day. And no one would be trapped in poverty because their land is valuable - that value is an asset she can borrow against or sell.

We have tried for 100 years to make complex taxes fair. We have failed. The code only grows more complex, more evaded, and more hated.

There is a better way. Stop taxing people for what they produce, and start collecting for the public what the public produces. Let labor keep all it earns. Let capital keep all it earns. Let land - the common birthright of all humanity - pay for our common needs.

A 100% Land Value Tax is not just tax reform. It is the restoration of a simple, ancient truth: we all have an equal right to the Earth, and a full right to the fruits of our labor.

If you tax labor, people may work less. If you tax buildings, people build less. If you tax land, the amount of land stays exactly the same. The tax cannot be passed on to tenants as higher rent, because rent is already set by what the market will bear. Therefore LVT is considered a non-distortionary tax.

  • Eliminates speculation and land hoarding: Under the current system, an owner can hold valuable land vacant or underused while waiting for its price to go up. If the full annual rental value is taxed, holding land idle becomes expensive. Owners must either use it productively or sell to someone who will.

  • Encourages development and lowers housing costs: Because improvements are not taxed at all, there is no penalty for building more housing, renovating a building, or intensifying use. Georgists argue this increases supply of housing and commercial space, driving down their price. The price of land itself falls because its speculative value is eliminated.

  • Eliminates need for other taxes: George argued that land rent is so large that capturing all of it would be sufficient to fund government. By replacing taxes on income, sales, profits, and buildings, you remove all taxes that discourage production, saving, and investment.

  • Reduces boom-and-bust cycles: Georgists attribute real estate bubbles to land speculation. By removing the profit from speculation, they argue, price bubbles driven by land would be prevented.

  • Cannot be evaded and simple to administer: Land cannot be hidden in an offshore account or moved. Its location and boundaries are visible. Assessment is based on nearby comparable sales of land value, minus improvement value.

In short, the Georgist argument is: taxing labor and capital makes society poorer and less productive, while taxing land value recaptures a value that society created in the first place, without reducing the amount of land available.
